Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

صفحة 161
Surah Fatir

It is also called Surat al-Malaika (the Surah of the Angels). It is Meccan, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others. In Majma' al-Bayan, al-Hasan said: "It is Meccan except for two verses: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ [Fatir: 29] to the end of the verse, and ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾ [Fatir: 32] to the end of the verse." Its number of verses is forty-six according to the last Medinan and the Syrian reciters, and forty-five according to the rest. The connection (munasabah), according to al-Bahr, is that when Almighty and Majestic God mentioned at the end of the previous surah the destruction of the polytheists, the enemies of the believers, and their being brought down to the places of punishment, it became incumbent upon the believers to praise Him, exalted is He, and to thank Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. To this is added the kinship of the two surahs in beginning with praise (al-hamd), their closeness in length, and other things.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Praise be to Allah, Fatir of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the One who brings them into existence without a pattern to imitate or a rule to follow. Thus fatr means innovation (ibda'). Al-Raghib said: it is God's bringing a thing into existence and originating it in a form disposed toward a certain action.

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I did not know what Fatir of the heavens and the earth meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said: 'I am the one who fatartuha (originated it),' meaning I began it. The original meaning of fatr is splitting." Al-Raghib said: splitting lengthwise; then it was used metaphorically for what preceded, and it became widespread until it too became a literal meaning.

The connection: "the heavens and the earth," meaning by them the entire world, since they are contingent (mumkin), and the basic state of the contingent is non-existence, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], and as the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whatever Allah wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be." The philosophers of Islam stated this explicitly. Their chief said: "The contingent in itself is not [existent], and it is hopeless of its cause," as if non-existence is latent in them, and by their origination they are split and non-existence comes out of them.

It has been said regarding this: it is as if He, exalted is He, split non-existence by bringing them out from it. It has also been said: there is no obstacle to taking the word on its original sense here, and it would refer to the rains and plants, so it is as if it were said: "Praise be to Allah, Fatir of the heavens through the rains and Fatir of the earth through the plants." There is a discussion of this which will be pointed out shortly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ — on both views it may mean: Who made the angels, peace be upon them, intermediaries between Him and His prophets and righteous servants, conveying His message to them by revelation, inspiration and true dreams; or who made them intermediaries between Him and His creation, conveying to them the traces of His power and workmanship such as rains, winds and others, and these are the angels entrusted with the affairs of the world. This is more fitting with the second view, but it may be objected that there is no sense in the rains splitting the heavens. Al-Imam said: praise is for blessings, and God's blessings are both immediate and deferred. In Surah Saba' it refers to the blessing of origination and resurrection, and its indication is: ﴿He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends into it﴾ [Saba': 2; al-Hadid: 4], and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve say: The Hour will not come to us﴾ [Saba': 3]. Praise in this surah refers to the blessing of abiding in the Hereafter, and its indication is "Who made the angels messengers," that is, He makes them messengers who receive the servants of Allah, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿the angels will receive them﴾. So the meaning may be: Praise be to Allah, Splitter of the heavens and the earth on the Day of Resurrection, for the descent of souls from the heaven and the emergence of bodies from the earth, and Maker of the angels messengers on that day, receiving His servants. Accordingly, the beginning of this surah is connected to the end of what preceded, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as was done to their likes﴾ [Saba': 54] explains the cutting off of the hope of those who were in disquieting doubt. When He, exalted is He, mentioned their state, He mentioned the state of the believers and gave them good news of the sending of angels to them and that He, exalted is He, opens the doors of mercy for them. End. In it there is what there is of remoteness.

And ﴿Fatir﴾ is an attribute of Allah, and its idafah (genitive construction) is pure (mahdah). Abu al-Baqa said: because it refers to the past only. Others said: it is definite by the idafah, since it does not run on the verb but is intended for continuity and permanence, as one says: "Zayd, owner of slaves, has come," meaning: Zayd, who is of the nature of owning slaves, has come. Whoever holds that the idafah is not pure considers it an apposition (badal), which is rare in derivative nouns. The same applies to ﴿jai'l﴾ and ﴿rusulan﴾. On the view that its idafah is not pure, it governs the accusative by agreement. On the other view, it is so according to al-Kisa'i. Abu 'Ali held that it is in the accusative by a hidden verb that it indicates, because the active participle, when it has the sense of the past, does not govern according to him, like the rest of the Basrans, except when it has the definite article. Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi said: the active participle transitive to two objects governs the second, because by its idafah to the first, its idafah to the second became impossible, so its accusative is fixed for the second.

Some explained this by saying: by idafah it resembles the definite with the article, so it governs its action. This is on the assumption that the making (ja'l) is transformative (taslimi); but if it is originative (ibda'i), then "rusulan" is a circumstantial state (hal) that is anticipated (muqaddarah).

al-Dahhak and al-Zuhri read "fatara" and "ja'ala" as past-tense verbs, and put the following word in the accusative. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this may be on the assumption that alladhi is implied as an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, or on the assumption of qad, so the clause would be a circumstantial state.

But you know that the omission of the relative pronoun is not permitted according to the majority of the Basrans. The Kufans and al-Akhfash held that it is permitted, and Ibn Malik followed them, and in some of his books he stipulated that it be conjoined to another relative pronoun. Among their proofs is: "Believe in what (alladhi) was sent down to us and sent down to you," and Hassan's saying:

"Who among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah and supports him and praises him? They are equal."

And another's saying:

"Whoever his habit is caution and resolve, and whose desire he obeys, the two are equal."

Abu Hayyan preferred that the clause be the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "He is the one who fatara." And al-Hasan read "jai'lu" with the nominative as an expression of praise, with "al-mala'ika" in the genitive. 'Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu 'Amr read "jai'lu" with the nominative without tanwin and "al-mala'ika" in the accusative. He explained the omission of the tanwin as due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and the accusative of "al-mala'ika" when "jai'l" is for the past, according to the view of al-Kisa'i and Hisham on the permissibility of an attributive past participle governing the accusative. Ibn Ya'mur and Khulayd read "ja'ala" as a past-tense verb with "al-mala'ika" in the accusative, following their reading of "Fatir" like the majority, like the reading of one who read: ﴿Splitter of the morning, and He made the night a rest﴾ [al-An'am: 96]. In the Kashshaf, both "fatara" and "ja'ala" are read as past-tense verbs. al-Hasan and Humayd ibn Qays read "rusulan" with a sukun on the sin, and this is the dialect of Tamim.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿having wings, two, three, or four﴾ is an attribute of "rusulan." "Ulu" is a plural noun for "dhu," just as "ula" is a plural noun for "dha." A similar case among declinable nouns is "al-makhad." al-Jawhari said: they are the pregnant she-camels, singular khalifah. "Ajniha" is the plural of "janah," in the form of the plural of paucity, but the context requires that it denote multitude.

In al-Bahr: the analogical plural of multitude for it is "junuh," but if that was not heard, then "ajniha" is used for both few and many. The apparent meaning is that "janah" in its known sense among the Arabs is intended, but we do not know its reality and mode, and we do not say that it is made of feathers like the feathers of birds.

Indeed, Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the wings of the angels, peace be upon them, are downy. I have seen in some books of the Imamiyyah that the angels crowd in the assemblies of the Imams, so some of their feathers fall, and they gather them and make garments from them for their children. This, in my view, is a fabricated tale, and the mystics among them interpret it in a way that does not take it out of this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿two, two, three, three, four, four﴾ — the apparent view is that it is an attribute of "ajniha," and the prohibition of its declension, according to the well-known view, is due to its being an attribute and to the deviation (adl) from "

"two-two," "three-three" and "four-four." al-Zamakhshari said: these words are not declined only because of the repeated deviation in them, for they deviate from the forms of the numbers to other forms, as Umar deviated from Amir and Hizam from Hazimah, and from repetition to non-repetition, so there are two deviations. As for the attributiveness, the situation does not differ between the deviated and what it deviated from; do you not see that you say "I passed by women, four, and men, three," and no attention is paid to it. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that he analogized the attribute in this deviated form to the attribute in "arba'" and "thalathah," and this is not correct, because they did not count the mere attribute as a cause, but stipulated that the attributiveness be non-accidental, as in "arba'," and that it not accept the feminine ta', or that it be present in it, as in "thalath" and "thalathah." Sahib al-Kashf said regarding it: deviation from repetition is not considered for the form, and the deviation is considered in establishing the adl; then the deviation from the original form to express repetition, so there are not two deviations in any respect. And after granting that what is considered in the attribute is its concurrence with the placing of the deviated form, its accidental occurrence in the form deviated from does no harm. There is no direction to the prohibition, and no reliance on the authority, and this is the view of Sibawayh as transmitted by al-Jawhari, and it is the established view as I have pointed out. End. Sahib al-Fara'id and Sahib al-Taqrib also criticized him by the accidental occurrence of attributiveness in the deviated-from form and its absence in the deviated form. But al-Tibi said: I found in the words of some Maghribis a statement that may serve as an answer to it, namely that "thalath," for example, cannot be free of either being placed for the attribute without consideration of number, or not being so. If the first, then there is no number in it, and the presumed opposite is not so; if the second, then the attribute is accidental to "thalath" just as it is accidental to "thalathah." It may therefore be said that these numbers are not declined because of the repeated deviation, like the plural and the two feminine endings. End. In it there is what is not hidden.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these words were deviated in the state of indefiniteness, so they became definite by the deviation, and so they are not declined because of the deviation and the definiteness. This is a strange view, mentioned in al-Bahr as belonging to some Kufans. In the Kashshaf: they are indefinites that become definite with the definite article; you say "fulan yankihu al-muthanna wal-thula'h wal-ruba'" ("so-and-so marries in pairs, threes and fours"). It has been said that "mathna" and so on are circumstantial states (hal) of an omitted word, and the governing element is an omitted word indicating it.

"Rusulan": that is, they are sent in pairs, threes and fours. What is relied upon is what has preceded. The intended meaning is those having multiple wings differing in number according to the differences in their ranks by which they descend and ascend, or hasten when they are commanded. It is possible that the wings are for all or some of them for other purposes, such as adornment among themselves, and as lowering over the face out of modesty before Allah, exalted is He, and other things. The meaning is that among the angels there is a kind with two wings for each one, a kind with three wings for each one, and a kind with four wings for each one. The verse gives no indication of negating more; rather, some scholars said: the number mentioned is for indicating multiplicity and variety, not for specification, nor for negating a deficiency below two.

It has been transmitted by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ (53:18), that he saw Jibril (Gabriel) with six hundred wings. Al-Tirmidhi also transmitted from Masruq, from A'ishah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not see Jibril in his true form except twice: once at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and once in a form with six hundred wings, which filled the horizon."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "I came across in some books that there is a class of angels (peace be upon them) who have six wings: two wings with which they wrap their bodies, two wings with which they fly in some matter of Allah's affairs, and two wings drooping over their faces out of modesty before Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Inquiry into how the wings are arranged, whether in pairs or singly, is, in my view, of no benefit, and nothing has been authentically established for me on this matter. Some have also argued by analogy of the unseen to the seen, saying: the meaning is that on each side some angels have two wings, some have three, and some have four; otherwise, if one had three, it would not be balanced. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

Some people said: the "wing" is a reference to direction. Its explanation is that Allah, Exalted, has nothing above Him, and everything other than Him is under His power, glorified is He. The angels (peace be upon them) have a direction towards Allah, Exalted, from which they take His bounties and give to those beneath them what they have taken, by His permission, glorified is He, as the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾ (26:193-194), and He said: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ (53:5), and He said: ﴿And those who arrange affairs﴾ (79:5). These are two wings. Among them are those who perform good deeds through an intermediary, and among them are those who perform it without an intermediary. So among the intermediaries, one has three directions, and another has four directions or more. This is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning, and the Sunni who holds that the angels (peace be upon them) are subtle luminous bodies, able to take various forms and to perform arduous acts, does not need it. It is needed only by the philosophers (Falasifah) and their followers, for in their view the angels are the immaterial intellects (al-'uqul al-mujarradah). The Ahl al-Ishraq (Illuminationists) call them "the manifest lights," and some Sufis call them "the luminous pavilions." Some of their later scholars mentioned that they have real essences and relational essences, related to what is below them as the soul is related to the body. As for their real essences, these are purely of the command, the decree and the word; and as for their relational essences, these are of creation and of destiny, from which arise the angels of the Preserved Tablet (al-lawhiyyah), the greatest of whom is Israfil (peace be upon him). According to them, the term "angels" is also applied to things other than intellects, such as the upper and lower "regulating" forces of souls and natures. They prolonged discussion of this, but the apparent meanings of the verses and the reports refute them. And Allah, Exalted, is the One who grants success in what is correct.

﴿He increases in creation what He wills﴾: this is a resumed statement confirming what precedes it regarding the variation among the angels (peace be upon them) in the number of wings, and indicating that this is one of the rulings of His will, Exalted, not due to any matter pertaining to their essences. It states a general rule, clearly indicating that He, Mighty and Majestic, increases in any creation whatever He wills to increase, according to what His will requires and what His wisdom demands, glorified is He, among matters which description cannot encompass. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: this refers to the wings that the angels have, that is, He increases in the creation of the wings of the angels whatever He wills, so He makes each one have six wings or more. This is also narrated from al-Hasan. It seems the clause is to dispel the assumption that there is no increase beyond four.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "He increases in the creation of the angels and their wings what He wills." It has also been said: "creation" (al-khalq) refers to the creation of man, and "what He wills" is: good form, or a good voice, or good fortune, or beauty in the two eyes, or in the nose, or in the face, or lightness of spirit, or curliness and beauty of hair, or intellect, or knowledge, or craftsmanship, or chastity in poverty, or sweetness of speech. They mentioned in some of these some prophetic reports (akhbar marfu'ah). The truth is that all of this is by way of illustration, not restriction, and the verse encompasses all of that, indeed it encompasses what is apparently considered beautiful and what is not considered beautiful, and everything from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is good.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾: this is an explanation, by way of verification, of the stated ruling, for the comprehensiveness of His power over all things is something that necessarily entails His power, glorified is He, to increase in every creation whatever He wills, clearly necessitating it.

﴿Mā yaftaḥi Allāhu lil-nāsi min raḥmatin﴾: that is, what Allah releases and sends forth. The "opening" (fatḥ) is a figurative usage (majāz) for sending, through the relation of causality (ʿalāqah sababiyyah), since opening what is closed is the cause of releasing what is in it and sending it forth. For this reason it is contrasted with "withholding" (imsāk) and "releasing" (iṭlāq), as a metonymy (kināyah) for giving. As it is said, "The sultan released (uṭliqa) the soldiers' stipends (arzāqahum)," so this is a metonymy branching from the figurative usage.

In the choice of the word "opening" there is a hint that mercy is among the most precious treasures and the hardest to attain. Its indefiniteness (tankīr) is for generality and vagueness, meaning: whatever mercy Allah, exalted is He, opens from the treasuries of His mercy, of whatever kind, whether blessing, health, security, knowledge, wisdom, or other things that cannot be encompassed, so much so that ʿUrwah used to say, as Ibn al-Mundhir related from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr from him, concerning riding the litter (al-maḥmal): "By Allah, it is a mercy that has been opened to the people," and then he would recite: ﴿What Allah opens to the people of mercy...﴾, etc.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim related from al-Suddī: "The mercy is the rain," and from Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is repentance." The intended meaning is illustration (tamthīl). The prepositional phrase "min raḥmah" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), not in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah), because the conditional noun (ism al-sharṭ) cannot be qualified.

﴿Fa-lā mumsika lahā﴾: that is, no one is able to withhold it. ﴿Wa-mā yumsik﴾: that is, whatever He withholds. ﴿Fa-lā mursila lah﴾: that is, no one is able to send it forth. The difference between the two pronouns is because the referent of the first is specified by "mercy," while the referent of the second is general, encompassing it and other things. Together with the fronting of the matter of opening mercy, this indicates that His mercy, exalted is He, precedes His wrath, as is reported in the authentic hadith. It was also said: the meaning is "and what He withholds of mercy," but the specifier was omitted because what precedes indicates it. The masculine form is considered in light of the wording, and there is nothing that strengthens considering the meaning in pronunciation. This is supported by the reading "fa-lā mursila lahā" with the feminine pronoun.

﴿Min baʿdihi﴾: that is, after His withholding it. ﴿Wa-huwa al-ʿazīz﴾: the Overpowering, dominant over all that He wills of matters, among which are opening and withholding. ﴿Al-Ḥakīm﴾: the One who does everything He does in accordance with what wisdom and benefit require. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) confirming what precedes it and indicating that each of the opening and the withholding is in accordance with the wisdom upon which the affair of creation turns. How compelling this verse is toward turning exclusively to Allah, exalted is He, turning away from all else, and easing the heart from imaginings that cause anxiety and sleepless nights.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays, who said: "Four verses of the Book of Allah, exalted is He: when I recite them, I do not care what I wake up to or what I go to sleep with: ﴿What Allah opens to the people of mercy, none can withhold it, and what He withholds, none can send it after Him﴾, and ﴿If Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He, and if He intends good for you, there is none to repel His bounty﴾ [Yunus: 107], and ﴿Allah will bring, after hardship, ease﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 7], and ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hūd: 6]."

Having shown that He, glory be to Him, is the originator of dominion and the realm of the unseen, and that He disposes of them absolutely, He commanded all people, or, as Ibn Abbas narrated and al-Tibi preferred, the people of Mecca, to give thanks for His blessings, may He be mighty and majestic. So He said: ﴿O mankind, remember the blessing of God upon you﴾. That is, His bounty, may He be blessed and exalted, upon you, if "blessing" (ni'mah) is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), or "that which is upon you" if it is taken as a noun (ism). The meaning is: observe it and preserve it by knowing its due, acknowledging it, and devoting worship and obedience to the One who bestowed it. Therefore the intended meaning is not merely mentioning it with the tongue. Rather, it is a metonymy (kinayah) for what has been mentioned.

From Ibn Abbas, with the address directed to those who hear you: ﴿remember the blessing of God upon you﴾, in that He settled you in His sanctuary and protected you from the whole world, while people are snatched away from around you. Also from him: the blessing of God, exalted is He, is well-being (al-'afiyah). The better view is not to restrict it to one meaning.

Since the blessings of God, exalted is He, though their kinds are many, are confined to the blessing of origination (al-ijad) and the blessing of continuance (al-ibqa'), He, glory be to Him, negated that there exists in existence anything other than Him that issues either of the two blessings. He did so by way of interrogation, which is used to deny assent and to reject a judgement. So He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾ Does hal (هل) come for this purpose? As is found in al-Mutawwal and its glosses, yes. As for al-Radi's statement that hal is not used for denial, he meant denial directed against one who claims that the event has occurred, as in the verse ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons?﴾ (al-Isra, 40). This entails negation and denial directed against one who asserts that the thing happened. It is like your saying: "Do you strike Zayd while he is your brother?" That is: is there a creator, distinct from Him, existing for you or for the world?

The word ﴿creator﴾ (khaliq) is the subject (mubtada') with a deleted predicate. The particle min was added to it to emphasise generality. ﴿Other than God﴾ (ghayru Allah) is a qualifier (sifah) of it according to its grammatical position. Qualifying with it is valid even though it is attached to the most definite of definites, because it is so thoroughly indefinite that it does not acquire definiteness in such a construction.

It is also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for ﴿creator﴾, on that same basis. The denial is treated as negation, so that "other than God" is the negated creator. Also, the meaning is by way of exception: there is no creator except God, and substitution after exception with ghayr is only valid in a negative statement. On this basis, min was added according to the majority of grammarians, and it became valid to begin with an indefinite noun.

Likewise it is permitted that it be the agent (fa'il) of khaliq, because it relies on the interrogative particle, as in "Is there a standing man, Zayd?" in one of its two readings. In that case it takes the place of the predicate. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying: "There is a problem here, namely that an active participle, or what functions like it, when it relies on an interrogative particle and is treated as a verb, so that it governs what follows it as its subject, can it be preceded by min of universality, so that one says 'Is there any standing men, Zayd and his companions?' as you say 'Is there standing Zayd and his companions?' Apparently it is not permitted. Do you not see that when it is treated as a verb there is no generality in it, unlike when min enters upon it? I do not know a parallel in the speech of the Arabs, and one should not proceed to permit such a thing except on the basis of attested usage from their speech." He replied: "The condition for addition and for operation is present, and he has not indicated any valid impediment to rely on. So hesitation is obstinacy without genuine reason."

In al-Kashf: there is no obstacle to ghayr being a predicate. Al-Shihab denied it, saying the meaning does not accord with it. Ibn Wathhab, Shaqiq, Abu Ja'far, Zayd ibn Ali, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ghayri﴾ in the genitive, as a qualifier of khaliq according to its wording. In this reading that is necessary. Since agreement between the two readings is better than disagreement, the more apparent reading in the first recitation is that it is also a qualifier of khaliq. Al-Fadl ibn Ibrahim al-Nahwi read ﴿ghayra﴾ in the accusative, as an exception.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He provides you with sustenance from the heaven and the earth﴾, through rain and plants, it is a new independent sentence (kalam mubtada') with no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case). It is not a qualifier of ﴿khaliq﴾ either by its wording or its position. In al-Kashf he said: because the meaning is reproach and reminder with what they acknowledge. It is as if it were said: "Is there any creator of those blessings you were commanded to remember, or in general?" The latter is better. ﴿Other than God﴾ enters primarily. Then He completed this by saying that He provides you with sustenance from the heaven and the earth, and that too requires that worship be exclusively His, just as creatorship requires it. In it is this point: the creator is only one who provides sustenance. If it had been said, "Is there any creator who provides sustenance from the heaven and the earth other than God?", the statement would depart from its intended course.

It is also permitted that ﴿khaliq﴾ be the agent of an implied verb which the mentioned verb explains. The original would be: "Does a creator provide you with sustenance?", with min being an extra particle in the agent. This was objected to: if what is in the sublime text is of the type "Hal rajulun 'urifa" (Is a man known?), then al-Sakkaki clearly stated that this construction is ugly, because hal enters only upon a declarative sentence, so the sentence must be valid before hal enters it. "A man is known" is not valid without considering inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), since there is no other valid basis for the beginning with an indefinite noun. When inversion is considered, the sentence conveys assent to the act itself, so hal cannot enter it, because hal seeks assent, and what has been attained is not sought, lest it entail obtaining what is already obtained. And there is the possibility that rajul is the agent of a deleted verb. He described it as ugly, not impossible.

If it is of the type "Hal Zayd 'urifa" (Is Zayd known?), then the second scholar, al-Sa'd al-Taftazani, explicitly stated that it is ugly by the agreement of the grammarians, and that what the author of al-Mufassal mentioned, that "Hal Zayd kharaja" (Did Zayd go out?) is on the assumption of a deleted verb, is an justification of a weak and remote reading, not something common and good. The only point is that the cause of its ugliness is not what al-Sakkaki mentioned regarding "Hal rajul 'urifa", since that does not apply here. Rather the cause is that hal, originally, has the meaning of qad (indeed), and its original form is ahal, as in the verse:

"Have you recognised the abode at the two Ghurrah?"

The omission of the hamzah before it is due to its frequent occurrence in interrogation. So it itself took the place of the hamzah and attached itself to it in interrogative use. Qad is among the particles that belong with verbs, and so likewise is what has its meaning. It was not deemed ugly for it to enter upon a nominal sentence whose two parts are nouns, because when it does not see a verb in its domain, it forgets it and is consoled. This differs from when it sees the verb, for then it recalls old times of the fever, longs for the familiar companion, and seeks to embrace him, and does not accept the separation of the noun between them.

From this it becomes known that there is no difference among the grammarians between "Hal rajul 'urifa" and "Hal Zayd ta'rifu" in ugliness for this reason. Some answered that the one who permitted this aspect was al-Zamakhshari and his followers, and he does not concede what was mentioned, because the conditional particle was in the example obligatory for the verb from hal, since it is not permitted for it to enter a nominal sentence whose two parts are nouns, as hal entered it. The operation of the verb after it, under the condition of interpretation, has been permitted without ugliness, as in His saying: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ (al-Tawbah, 6). So it is permitted with hal by a stronger argument.

It was also said: it is permitted that ﴿He provides you﴾ and what follows be a resumptive sentence in answer to an implied question whose supposed form is: "What creator is it about whom one asks?" And that it be the predicate of khaliq. It is not hidden from one who reflects that what was quoted from al-Kashf indicates the inferiority of all these aspects. So reflect.

In the verse, according to what is the better view in its interpretation and grammatical analysis, there is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah in their saying that the servant creates his own actions. And there is support for the people of the Sunnah in their saying: there is no creator except God, exalted is He.

﴿There is no god but He﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming the negation understood from what preceded, deliberately. Jar Allah did not permit that it be made a qualifier of khaliq, as ﴿He provides you﴾ was made a qualifier of it. He said: "If the clause ﴿there is no god but He﴾ were connected as ﴿He provides you﴾ was connected, the meaning would not support it. Because your saying, 'Is there any other creator besides God? There is no god but that creator', is not correct. For your saying, 'Is there any creator besides God?' is an affirmation of God, exalted is He. So if you went on to say that, you would be contradicting by negating after affirming." The author of al-Kashf explained the aspect of contradiction on the assumption that "other than God" is a qualifier: the statement is directed to negate partnership in the actual attribute, namely creation. So your saying, 'Is there any other creator besides God?', is an affirmation of God, exalted is He, and a negation of a partner to Him in it. Then describing the other with the restriction of divinity to him would be to negate his creatorship, not to make him singular in divinity. Singularity in divinity together with being distinct from God, exalted is He, are contradictory, because the first negates it from Him, exalted is He, to an exceedingly great degree, and the second affirms it alongside another, while He is far above every partner and deficiency. Then he said: "The verification of this is that hal is for denying what follows it, and what follows it, if it is part of its completion, the judgement of denial extends to what remains. Otherwise it is left in its state of negation and affirmation. Since the discussion concerns creatorship as has passed, the two attributes, namely the singularity of the other in divinity and his distinction from the Self-Subsisting, True One, do not become its object. Both are contradictory in themselves as has been explained. So what Jar Allah mentioned necessarily follows, clearly." End of quotation.

This objection has been answered by that formulation, removing much dispute, but it is not free from scrutiny. The contradiction can be stated on the assumption of the qualifying function in a clearer way, which perhaps is not hidden from one who reflects. It is also possible that what prevents the qualifying function is the inimitable composition of the text, whose judge is sound taste. The discussion on this is long, so reflect.

The fa' in His saying: ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ (fa-anna tu'fakun) is for ordering the denial of their turning away from monotheism to polytheism, based on what precedes it. As if it were said: "Since His singularity in divinity, creatorship and provision has become clear, from what direction are you turned away from monotheism to polytheism?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], then were messengers denied before you﴾ etc., is a consolation to him, peace and blessings be upon him, with the general nature of the trial, a promise to him (ﷺ) and a warning to his enemies. The meaning is: And if they persist in denying you regarding what you have conveyed to them of the clear truth, after you have established the proof against them and silenced them with the argument, then take as your model (ta'assa) those messengers in patience, for their peoples denied them and they were patient.

So the clause ﴿messengers were denied before you﴾ stands in the place of the answer to the conditional, while the answer in reality is "take as your model" (ta'assa). That clause has been put in its place, by mentioning the cause instead of the effect. It is also permitted that the clause itself be the answer without any supposed omission, and that what follows from the condition is the informing and the telling, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [An-Nahl: 53].

The indefinite form "messengers" (rusul) is for magnification and multiplicity, which entail greater consolation and an incitement to take as a model and to be patient over what befell him, peace and blessings be upon him, from his people; that is, messengers of great station and great number.

﴿And to Allah are returned the matters﴾, not to any other, Mighty and Majestic is He, so that He, glory be to Him, will recompense each of you and them with what befits Him. In limiting the return to Him, exalted is He, together with the vagueness of the recompense, whether reward or punishment, there is an emphasis on promise and warning that is not hidden. It was also read "turja'u" (تَرْجِعُ) with a fatha on the ta', from the return (ruju'), and the first reading is more effective in inspiring awe.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 5:**

﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah﴾ referred to by His words, glorified is He, ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (from resurrection (ba'th) and recompense (jaza')) ﴿is true﴾, established without doubt, without any failure to fulfil it. ﴿So do not let the worldly life deceive you﴾, namely, let the enjoyment of its provisions distract you and its amusements with its adornments preoccupy you, so that you neglect to prepare what would benefit you on the day the appointed time arrives. The intended meaning is the prohibition against being deceived by it, even though the prohibition is grammatically directed at it, like the words of His, exalted is He: ﴿Let not my dissension lead you into sin﴾ [Hud: 89], and your saying, "Let me not see you here." ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾, since He, majestic is His glory, is the Pardoner, the Generous, the Compassionate, the Merciful. ﴿The Deceiver﴾, that is, the one who is most extreme in deception. According to what has been related from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid, this is Satan, so the definite article is for a specific reference (al-'ahd). It is also permissible that it be generic (al-ta'mim), meaning: let not every one whose nature is to be extreme in deception deceive you, by making you hope for forgiveness while persisting in disobedience, saying that Allah forgives all sins. Although that is possible, engaging in sins with this expectation is like taking poison, relying on the body's ability to expel it. The repetition of the prohibition verb is for emphasis, and because the two deceptions differ in manner.

Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sammal read «اَلْغُرُورُ» with a *damma*, on the basis that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of *gharrahu yaghurruhu*, although this form is rare for a transitive verb; or it is a plural of *gharr* (one who deceives), like *qu'ud* and *sujud*, which can be both a verbal noun and a plural. If it is taken as a verbal noun, the attribution of the action is metaphorical (majazi).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾: an enmity that is general and ancient, which hardly ever ceases. This is indicated by the nominal sentence, and by "to you" (lakum), with its being placed first for emphasis. ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾ by opposing him in your beliefs and your actions, and be on guard against him in all the circumstances of your lives.

﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾: this confirms his enmity and warns against obeying him, by alerting that his purpose in calling his followers to follow desire and to incline toward the pleasures of this world is nothing but to ruin them and cast them into everlasting punishment, from where they do not perceive. So the lam (in liyakunu) is not the lam of consequence (al-'aqibah, indicating an outcome), although Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that it is.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 7:

﴿Those who disbelieve, for them is a severe punishment﴾ because of their disbelief and their response to the call of Satan and their following of his footsteps. Perhaps the indefiniteness of "punishment" (ʿadhāb) is for its magnification in terms of duration, as if it was said: "For them is a lasting, severe punishment."

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness﴾ great ﴿and a great reward﴾ with no limit to either of them, because of what has been mentioned of faith and righteous action.

(Alladhīna kafarū) is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿for them is a punishment﴾, and likewise (alladhīna āmanū) and ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾, etc. Some scholars permitted ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ to be in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿companions of the Blaze﴾ or as its qualifier (ṣifah), or in the accusative position as a substitute for ﴿his party﴾ or as its qualifier, or in the nominative position as a substitute for the pronoun in (li-yakūnū). All of these undermine the eloquence of the composition, as is not hidden from the discerning.

[p. 168]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 35, verse 8:

﴿Is then one to whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, so that he sees it as good?﴾ That is, his evil deed was made good in his eyes, ﴿so that he sees it﴾, that is, believes it, because of the beautification, ﴿as good﴾. Here the attribute is attached to the thing it describes (idafat al-sifah ila al-mawsuf, "the attribute annexed to its qualified noun"), and ﴿man﴾ (whoever) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'). The sentence after it is its relative clause (sila), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. The ﴿fa'﴾ indicates a consequence (lil-tafri', "for deduction"), and the ﴿hamzah﴾ is interrogative for denial (lil-inkar, "for rejection"). If the interrogative is placed before its original position through an inversion of order (min ta'khir, "by postponement"), as is the view of Sibawayh and the majority in such cases, then the intent is to derive the denial of what follows from the two rulings that precede it. That is: if the end of each of the two groups is what has been mentioned, then the one for whom disbelief was made attractive by their enemy Satan, so that he believed it good and immersed himself in it, is not like the one who found it repugnant, avoided it, and chose faith and righteous deeds.

[p. 169]

If, however, it remains in its original place, and the conjunction is upon an implied element, into which it enters, as a group of scholars held, then the intent is what falls within its scope. The meaning would be: ﴿أهما﴾ (are they?), that is, those who disbelieved and those who believed and did righteous deeds, are equal? Then the one for whom disbelief was made attractive by the enemy Satan, so that he believed it good and immersed himself in it, is not like the one who found it repugnant, avoided it, and chose faith and righteous deeds. That is, they are not equal, so that the one for whom disbelief was made attractive is like the one who found it repugnant. This predicate has been omitted because the context indicates it and the sublime structure of the speech requires it. Both parts have been stated explicitly in a parallel verse, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then one who has clear evidence from his Lord like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive?﴾ [Muhammad: 14], and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Is then one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19], and His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose likeness is in darknesses?﴾ [al-An'am: 122].

In describing the disbeliever as ﴿one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive so that he sees it as good﴾, there is an indication of the extreme extent of his error, to the point that it is as if it has overpowered his intellect and deprived him of discernment. The condition of one overpowered in his intellect is like this, as the verse of Abu Nuwas indicates:

*Give me to drink until you see me as good, while the ugly is beautiful to me.*

The apparent sense of al-Zajjaj's words is that ﴿man﴾ is a conditional (shartiyyah), since he said: "The answer (jawab) is of two kinds. One of them is what His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so do not let yourself go﴾, etc. indicates, and the meaning would be: 'Is one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, so Allah has sent him astray, your soul would have gone out in regret over them?' The second is what His saying, exalted is He, ﴿indeed Allah﴾, etc. indicates, and the meaning would be: 'Is one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive like one whom Allah has guided?'" Ibn Malik also took this view. Ibn Hisham objected to the second estimate, saying that an adverbial phrase (zarf) cannot be an answer even if we consider it a clause, and the reason is that al-Radi stated that it cannot be stable (mustaqirr) except in the position of predicate, adjective, relative clause, or circumstantial (hal), and the answer was not mentioned. This is not because of the absence of the ﴿fa'﴾, whose estimate is that it enters upon a subject (mubtada') of which the adverbial phrase is the predicate, and the whole clause as an answer is not permissible because of the artificiality involved, as has been said.

Some have claimed that it is permissible for al-Zajjaj to have held that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, and that the answer is applied to its predicate because of its resemblance to it in meaning. Do you not see that they insert the ﴿fa'﴾ into the predicate of a relative pronoun whose relative clause is a verbal sentence, just as they insert it into the answer of a conditional, so they say: "Whoever comes to me, then for him is a dirham"? In this, however, there is departure from the apparent meaning, and there is no evidence for intending it except the invalidity of the conditional character. The first estimate was deemed weak because of the separation between the place of omission and the indicator of the omitted element, together with the obscurity of the connection of the clause with what precedes it. It is not appropriate for ﴿man﴾ to be conditional with ﴿fa-ra'ahu﴾ as its answer, because of the awkwardness this involves in terms of grammatical construction (rakakah sina'iyyah), since the past tense in the answer is not joined to the ﴿fa'﴾ without ﴿qad﴾, together with the obscurity of the matter of denying the seeing of evil as good after the beautification, and its consequence upon what precedes it of the two rulings. The denial being because the one who beautified it is Satan, the enemy, and the consequence upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party to be among the companions of the Blaze﴾, is not hidden in its condition. So the reliable view is the one mentioned earlier, and attention should be given to it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ is an explanation for the causal role of the beautification in seeing the ugly as good. In it there is a removal of the improbability that a person should see the ugly as good through the enemy's beautifying it for him, by making clear that this is by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, which follows His knowledge concerning things as they are in reality. It is also a notice that those disbelievers for whom the evil of their deeds was made attractive, so that they saw it as good, are among those whom Allah, exalted is He, has willed to be astray.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not let yourself go in regret over them﴾ is a consequence of this. That is: if the matter is as such, then do not let yourself go, etc. Mawla Sa'di Jalabi mentioned that the ﴿hamzah﴾ in ﴿Is then one﴾, according to the first of the two estimates reported from al-Zajjaj, is for denying that the Prophet ﷺ's soul would go out in regret over them. The ﴿fa'﴾ in His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿indeed Allah﴾, etc. is for explaining what the sublime structure implies, that there is no benefit in grief. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the two groups, those who disbelieved and those who believed, He said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive so that he sees it as good?﴾, meaning: Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive from these two groups like one for whom it has not been made attractive? So it is as if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "No." Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, so do not let yourself go in regret over them﴾.

It is understood from the words of al-Tibi that the ﴿fa'﴾ of ﴿so do not let yourself go﴾ is a conditional consequence (jaza'iyyah), and the ﴿fa'﴾ of ﴿indeed Allah﴾ is for causation (lil-ta'lil), and that the clause is preposed from a postponed position. He said: "He ﷺ was eager for the faith of the people and that he should place the astray in the company of the guided. So it was said to him, peace and blessings be upon him, by way of denial of that: 'Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive from these two groups like one for whom it has not been made attractive?' Then he must affirm the negation and say, 'No.' At that point it is said to him: 'If that is so, then do not let yourself go in regret over them, for Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.'" So he preposed and postponed. This is finished. There is room for examination in this. The verses, according to what the apparent words of al-Zamakhshari require, contain a laff wa-nashr (an arrangement in which two items are mentioned and then each is matched to its corresponding item), and al-Tibi explicitly stated this. He then said: "It is better to take the verses as involving jam' (gathering), taqsim (division), and tafriq (separation). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾ gathers the two groups together under the address to mankind, and gathers what they have of reward and punishment under the ruling of promise, and warns them both together against being deceived by the world and by Satan. As for division, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment, and those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾. As for separation, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾, because in it He separated and made clear the difference between the two groups." Just as al-Zamakhshari said: "Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive from these two groups like one for whom it has not been made attractive?" From this he derived that the ﴿fa'﴾ in ﴿Is then one﴾ is for sequence (lil-ta'qib), and that the ﴿hamzah﴾ placed between the conjoined and the element it is conjoined to is for denying equality and establishing the great gulf between the two groups. He also said that the preferred view among several options mentioned by al-Sakkaki in *al-Miftah* is to estimate "like one whom Allah has guided", which is omitted because of the indication of ﴿Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. They have a lengthy discussion on the arrangement of the noble verses other than what we have mentioned. Whoever wishes it should consult the books of tafsir and of Arabic grammar. Perhaps in what we have mentioned there is sufficiency for one who has been given a sound mind and a correct understanding.

[p. 170]

*Al-hasarat* is the plural of *hasrah*, which is grief over what has been lost and regret for it, as if the one who experiences it is exhausted by what drove him to commit it, or his strength has been exhausted from excessive sorrow, or weariness has overtaken him so that he cannot make up for what he has neglected. It is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, "object of purpose"), that is: do not let yourself perish for the sake of regrets. The plural is used although *al-hasrah* in origin is a verbal noun that applies to the few and the many, to indicate the multiplication of the Prophet ﷺ's sorrow over their condition, or because of the abundance of their ugly deeds, which necessitate lamentation and regret. ﴿Over them﴾ is a complement (silah) of ﴿go﴾, as one says "he perished out of love for him" and "he died out of sorrow for him." Or it is an explanation of the object of regret, in which case it is a stable adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr), and its governed element is omitted, as if it were said: "Over whom do you go?" and it was answered: "Over them." It is also permitted that it be connected to ﴿hasarat﴾, on the basis that a complement of a verbal noun may precede it when it is an adverbial phrase. This is what I prefer, although al-Zamakhshari does not permit it. It is also permitted that ﴿hasarat﴾ be a circumstantial accusative (hal) from ﴿nafsuka﴾, as if all of it became regrets because of the intensity of grief, as Jarir said:

*The hot desert winds wore away their flesh along with the night journey, until they departed as breastbones and chests.*

He means: they returned as breastbones and chests, that is, nothing remained but their breastbones and chests. This is the view Sibawayh adopted for the verse. Al-Mubarrad said: "*kalakilan wa-suduran* is a specification (tamyiz) transferred from the subject, that is, until their breastbones and chests departed." From this is His saying:

*So after them my soul falls away in regrets, and their remembrance of me is a sickness.*

In this there are three exaggerations.

Ubayd ibn Umayr read ﴿zayyana﴾ in the active voice, and put ﴿sau'a﴾ in the accusative. It is also reported from him ﴿as'a'﴾ in the form of ﴿af'ala﴾, and by ﴿as'a'﴾ is meant their deed, namely polytheism. Talha read ﴿Aman﴾ without the ﴿fa'﴾. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: "The ﴿hamzah﴾ is for interrogation and confirmation, and it is also permitted that it be for calling, and what it calls for is omitted, that is: reflect and return to Allah, for indeed Allah, etc." The apparent sense is that it is for denial, as in the reading of the majority. Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Isa, al-Ashhab, Shayba, Abu Haywa, Humayd, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿tudhhib﴾ from ﴿adhhaba﴾, with ﴿nafsaka﴾ as the object in the accusative. It was also transmitted from Nafi'.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ This is in the position of a justification for what precedes it, and in it there is a warning to the disbelievers: that He, exalted is He, knows the ugly things they do, and so He will recompense them for them. The verses from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is then one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾ up to here were revealed, according to what is reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning Abu Jahl and the polytheists of Mecca. Juwaybir reported from al-Dahhak that they were revealed concerning Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl, since Allah guided Umar and sent Abu Jahl astray.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 9:

﴿And Allah is the One who sends the winds﴾: a subject and predicate. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ibn Kathīr read *al-riḥ* (the singular). The present tense in His words ﴿so they stir up clouds﴾ is used to narrate a past situation, to bring that wondrous scene vividly to mind, which shows the perfection of power and wisdom. They often do this with a verb that carries some distinction and particularity, in a situation that is strange or that concerns the addressee, or for some other reason. From this is the saying of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran (a pre-Islamic poet):

Is there anyone to convey to the youths of Fahm
what I encountered at the Raḥā Biṭān?

That I saw the ghoul swooping
across a desert plain, smooth as a page,

so I said to her: "We are both lean from the land,
a traveller; leave me my place."

She lunged at me in a rush and swooped,
so I struck her with my hand, with a Yemeni polished blade,

and I struck her without dismay, and she fell
prostrate, on her hands and on her neck.

Because stirring up is a property specific to the winds, and an effect that in most cases does not separate from them, it does not exist except after their existence. Thus it is future relative to the sending. On this view the use of the present tense is on its literal and actual sense, without interpretation, because what is considered is the time of the judgment, not the time of speaking. The *fa'* (then) indicates that this follows without delay, and that is another matter.

It is also permitted that the bringing of what indicates the past and then what indicates the future is an indication of the continuity of the matter, and that it is not restricted to one time over another, since past and future cannot be true of one thing at once unless that is intended. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: the difference between the two verbs is because when the act of sending is ascribed to Allah, the Exalted, and what He does, glorified be He, happens by His saying, "Be" (*kun*) [al-Baqarah 2:117 and elsewhere], it does not remain in non-existence for a time or even a part of a time. So the past form is used rather than the future, because its occurrence is necessary and its coming into being is swift, as if it had already been. Also, He, exalted be He, has finished with all things; He determined the sending at known times and to specified places, and the determining is like the sending. As for the stirring up, which is ascribed to the winds, and they are formed in a time, He, glorified be He, said "stirs up" (*tuthīr*) with the future form. End of quotation.

I object to this with His words in surah al-Rum: ﴿Allah is the One who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾, and in surah al-A'raf: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf 7:57], where the sending is expressed in the present tense. So reflect.

﴿Then We drive it to a dead land﴾: a portion of land in which there is no vegetation. It is read *mayt* with lightened pronunciation, and both have one meaning according to the well-known view.

[Page 172]

In the *Kulliyyat* of Abu al-Baqa' al-Kafawi: *al-mayt* with lightened pronunciation is the one who has died, and *al-mayyit* with the doubled letter and *al-ma'it* is the one who has not yet died. He recited:

Whoever has a spirit is then dead,
and the dead is none but one who is carried to the grave.

What is relied upon is the well-known view.

﴿Then We bring to life by it the earth﴾: that is, by the rain descending from it, indicated by the clouds, since there is a mutual implication between them in the mind as in reality; or by the clouds, since they are the cause of the cause. The bringing to life of the earth is the growing of trees and herbage in it. ﴿after its death﴾: its drying and emptiness of that. The stating of the two verbs in the past form is to indicate certainty. Their ascription to the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*, the "We" of greatness), which points to exclusivity to Him, the Exalted, is because of the greater craftsmanship in them and to complete the likeness between the bringing to life of the earth and the resurrection, to which it is compared by His saying: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾, in full exclusivity to the divine power.

Al-Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He ascribed "sent" to the third person, and brought "I bring to life" to the first person, because in the first, He, glorified be He, made Himself known by one of the acts, which is the sending; then once He was known, He said, Exalted be He: "I am the One you knew: I drove the clouds and brought the earth to life." So in the first it was a making known through a wondrous act, and in the second it was a reminder of blessing, for the perfection of My blessing is the winds and the clouds by driving and bringing to life. And that, as you see, is far-fetched.

He, glorified be He, said: ﴿We bring to life by it the earth﴾ rather than ﴿We bring it to life﴾, that is, the dead land by it, making the bringing to life attached to the genus known to everyone, which is the earth; and because that is more suitable to the matter of the resurrection. He said: ﴿after its death﴾, although bringing to life implies that, because it indicates that the death of the earth to which the bringing to life is attached is known to them, and by this the force of the comparison is strengthened. So reflect.

According to what is in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), *al-nushur* (the resurrection) is the verbal noun of *nashara* (it was spread out), when the dead one comes to life. Al-A'sha said:

Until people say, at what they see:
"How wondrous, for the dead one who rises!"

In *al-Nihayah* of Ibn al-Athir it is said: "*nashara al-mayyit* yanshuru *nushuran*" when he lives after death, and "*anshara-hu* Allah" means He brought him to life. Al-Raghib said: it is said that Allah Most High "*nashara*" the dead and "*anshara*" him with the same meaning. The truth is that Allah's "*nashara*" the dead is a metaphor taken from *nashr al-thawb*, that is, spreading out the garment, as the poet said:

The calamities of your time folded you after spreading,
and likewise its calamities, folding and spreading.

The intended meaning of *al-nushur* here is the bringing to life of the dead on the Day of Reckoning. It is the subject, and the prepositional phrase before it is in the position of the predicate. It was said that the *kaf* (in *kadhalika*) is in the nominative position as a predicate: that is, "like that bringing to life which you witness is the bringing to life of the dead on the Day of Resurrection in the soundness of being within power and ease of accomplishment, with no difference between them at all except the alif in the first and not in the second."

Abu Hayyan said: The comparison occurs in several respects. Just as the dead earth accepts the life fitting to it, so the limbs accept life. Or just as the wind gathers the pieces of cloud, so Allah Most High gathers the parts of the limbs and the fragments of the dead. Or just as He, glorified be He, drives the rain to the dead land, He, Mighty and Majestic, drives the spirit and life to the body.

Some of them said: the comparison is in terms of the manner. Ibn Jarir and others related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: An angel will stand with the trumpet between heaven and earth and blow into it, and no creature in the heavens and the earth will remain except those whom Allah wills, but they will all die. Then Allah Most High will send from beneath the Throne water like the semen of men, and their bodies will grow from that water. He recited the verse. Then an angel will stand and blow into it, and every soul will go forth to its body.

In the hadith of Muslim, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, Most High, will send down a rain like a light drizzle, and it will cause people's bodies to grow."

[Page 173]

The growth of bodies from the coccyx (*'ajb al-dhanab*), according to what is reported in the narrations, and it has come that it does not decay. It is the bone at the bottom of the spine at the rump. Abu Zayd al-Waqwaqi said: it is a single atom (*jawhar fard*) that remains from this creation and does not change. There is no need to insist that it is a single atom.

Beyond this there are strange sayings about this coccyx. It was said: it is the material intellect (*al-'aql al-hayulani*); it was said: rather the hyle (*al-hayuli*). And from al-Ghazali: it is only the soul, and upon it the afterlife's creation is grown. And from al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn 'Arabi): it is the fixed essence of the human being (*al-'ayn al-thabit*). And from some of the theologians: it is the original constituent parts. Mulla Sadra al-Shirazi said in his *Asfar*: it is for us the imaginative faculty, because it is the last of the existences that arise in the human being from the natural, animal and vegetative powers, successive in coming into being for the human matter in this world, and it is the first of the existences arising in the afterlife creation. Then he explained this with what he explained, and indeed it is weaker than the spider's web and more frail. What is relied upon is what agrees with the understanding of the people of the language. And what need is there for interpretation after affirming the power of the King, the Judge, exalted be His majesty and great be His dominion.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Whoever desires honour﴾: honour (*al-izzah*) means nobility and inaccessibility to harm, from their saying *ard izaz*, meaning "hard land." The noun is definite for the category (*lil-jins*). The verse concerns the disbelievers, who sought strength through the idols, as the Exalted said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of honour﴾ [Maryam: 81]. As for those who believed with their tongues without their hearts being in agreement, they sought strength through the polytheists, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do they seek honour with them?﴾ [al-Nisa: 139]. The word *man* (whoever) is a conditional noun (*ism shart*), and what follows it is the conditional verb. The combination of *kana* (was) and *yurid* (desires) indicates the constancy and continuity of the desire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾ is the answer-indicator (*dalil al-jawab*). It is not valid to make it the answer itself, grammatically (*min haythu al-sina'ah*), because it lacks a pronoun referring back to *man*. The grammarians have said: there must be in the apodosis a pronoun referring to the conditional noun when it is not an adverb of time or place. The implied sense is: whoever desires honour, let him seek it from Allah, the Exalted, for to Allah alone, not to anyone else, belongs honour. He, glorified is He, disposes of it as He wills. Thus the cause is placed in the position of the effect, because seeking it from the One to whom it belongs, and in whose dominion all of it lies, is an effect of that (the sovereignty). The definiteness of *al-izzah* is for comprehensiveness (*lil-istighraq*), as indicated by ﴿all﴾, and its accusative case is that of the circumstantial state (*al-hal*). What is meant is the honour of this world and the Hereafter. The fronting of the predicate before the subject is for exclusivity (*lil-ikhtisas*), as we have indicated.

This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿But honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. This is because honour belongs to Allah alone in its essence, while the Messenger (ﷺ) has honour through his nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and the believers have honour through the Messenger, peace be upon him. It seems that the preposition is repeated to indicate this.

Some have estimated the answer to be: ﴿let him obey Allah﴾, and this is supported by what Anas narrated, as in *Majma' al-Bayan*, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Your Lord says every day: I am the Mighty (al-'Aziz). Whoever desires the honour of both abodes, let him obey the Mighty." Whoever estimated it as "let him seek it from Allah, the Exalted," said: seeking from Him, the Exalted, is only by obedience and submission.

From al-Farra' the meaning is: whoever desires to know honour, that is, the power to subdue, of whom it belongs, let him attribute it to Allah, the Exalted, for it belongs to Him alone. It was also said: the meaning is, whoever desires honour, that is, dominance, then he is defeated, because dominance belongs to Allah, the Exalted, alone, and it is not achieved except by Him, mighty and majestic. This was attributed to Mujahid. It was also said: the definiteness of the first *al-izzah* is also for comprehensiveness or for a known reference, and what is meant is the complete individual instance, and the meaning is: whoever desires all honour, or the complete instance of it, which is the honour not tainted by humiliation in any respect, then he will not attain it, for it belongs to Allah, the Exalted, alone. This view is better than the two views before it, but the most apparent of the views to me is the first, which is attributed to Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ and so on, is like an explanation of the way to attain honour and the path to reaching it, which is verbal and practical obedience. It was also said: it is an explanation that all honour belongs to Allah, the Exalted, and is in His hand, glorified is He, because it comes through obedience, and obedience is not counted unless it is accepted. It was also said: it is a resumption of speech (*istinaf kalam*). The first view is the one relied upon.

[p. 174]

*Al-kalim* (the words) is a collective noun of genus according to a group, whose singular is *kalimah*. The good word (*al-kalim al-tayyib*), according to *al-Kashshaf* and *al-Bahr*, from Ibn 'Abbas, is "There is no god but Allah." Its being good, as it was said, is that sound reason finds it pleasant and delightful, because it contains an indication of the Oneness of God (*tawhid*), which is the axis of salvation and the means to everlasting bliss. Or the Law finds it delightful, or the angels, peace be upon them. It was also said: it is a good thing that reason accepts and does not reject. The application of *al-kalim* to this, if its singular *kalimah* is taken in its true meaning, is apparent, since it includes several words. But describing it as good, in relation to other than the Glorious Name, is obscure, and perhaps this is due to the particular nature of the construction. If its singular here is *kalimah* in its figurative meaning, as in His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾ [al-An'am: 115; al-A'raf: 137], and ﴿No! It is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], and His saying, peace be upon him: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid," and their saying: "There is no god but Allah" is "the word of monotheism," and so on, to an uncountable extent.

So the application of *al-kalim* to that is because it is multiplied by the multiplicity of the speaker. It seems that the indication of the figurative meaning of *kalimah*, which applies to speech, is the description as good, based on the view that what is found pleasant and delightful is speech, not a bare *kalimah* which does not convey a judgment by which the soul is expanded or constricted. Or it may be said: the frequent application of *kalimah* to speech and its currency among them, to the point that some said, as al-Himsi related in the margins of *al-Tasrih* from some commentators on *al-Ajurrumiyyah*, that it is a linguistic reality that dispenses with the need for an indicator.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) that he explained the good word as the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: it is "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest," and this is the apparent meaning of a report related by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami from Abu Hurayrah.

It was also said: it is "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and blessed is Allah." This is the apparent meaning of a report related by a group from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Shahr ibn Hawshab that it is the Qur'an. It was also said: it is praise with good for the righteous believers. It was also said: it is the supplication in which there is no injustice. The Imam said, and I follow him: the chosen view is that it is every speech which is a remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, or which is for Allah, glorified is He, such as counsel and knowledge. As for what Mulla Sadra conveyed in his *Asfar*, that it refers to pure and purified souls, since the word is applied to the soul when it is such, as the Exalted said about 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿And His word which He directed to Maryam﴾ [al-Nisa: 171], then it should not be counted among the views of the commentators, as is not hidden.

The ascent of words to Him, the Exalted, is a metonymy (*majaz mursal*) for their acceptance, through the relation of necessity (*'alaqat al-luzum*), and a metaphor (*isti'arah*) by comparing acceptance to ascent. It is also permitted that *al-kalim* be taken as a metonymy for what is written in it, through the relation of inherence (*'alaqat al-hulul*). Or a noun may be understood: that is, "to Him ascends the record of the good word." Or its external existence here, and then its written existence in heaven, may be compared to ascent, and then the comparing term is applied to the compared term, and the verb derived from it, according to what is known in the metaphor of the derivative type (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*). It was also said: there is no barrier to considering the literal reality of ascent for the words, since Allah has the power to embody meanings. That ascent to Him, mighty and majestic, is among the ambiguous matters (*al-mutashabih*), and the discussion of it is well known. The statement after that is a metonymy for its acceptance and for giving attention to the status of its speaker. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is to convey exclusivity.

'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Sulami and Ibrahim recited *yusʿidu* (with a *damma* on the *yaa* and a *dhamma*... in the causative form from *asʿada*) with *al-kalam al-tayyiba* in the accusative. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Dahhak recited *yusʿidu* with a *damma* on the *yaa*, and he did not mention whether it was active or passive, nor the case of what follows it. In *al-Kashshaf*: it is also read *ilayhi yusʿadu al-kalim al-tayyib* in the passive voice, and *ilayhi yusʿidu al-kalima al-tayyiba* from *asʿada*, and the one who causes ascent (*al-musʿid*) is the man, that is, he causes the good word to ascend to Allah, mighty and majestic. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, recited ﴿ilayhi yasʿadu﴾ from *saʿida*, with *al-kalam* in the nominative.

﴿And righteous deed raises it﴾: the subject and predicate, according to the well-known view. There is disagreement about the subject of *yarfa'u* (raises). It was said: it is a pronoun referring to the righteous deed, and the pronoun of the object refers to *al-kalim*, meaning: righteous deed raises the good word. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Shahr ibn Hawshab, as Sa'id ibn Mansur and others related from him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained "righteous deed" as the performance of the obligatory duties, then he said: whoever remembers Allah, the Exalted, and performs His obligations, his deed carries the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, and so it ascends with it to Allah, the Exalted. But whoever remembers Allah, the Exalted, and does not perform His obligations, his speech is returned to his deed, and his deed is more fitting for him. Ibn 'Atiyyah criticized this, saying: this is a view that contradicts the belief of the People of the Sunnah, and it is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas. The truth is that the one who disobeys by abandoning his obligations, if he remembers Allah, the Exalted, and speaks a good word, it is recorded for him and accepted from him, but upon him is the burden of abandoning the obligations, and Allah, the Exalted, accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. End of quote.

Perhaps what is meant by the raising of the righteous deed of the good word is the raising of its rank and making it such that the reward that results from it is greater than what would result from it if it were without deed. The hadith: "Allah does not accept a word except with deed, and does not accept a word and deed except with intention, and does not accept a word, deed, and intention except when it accords with the Sunnah," which is mentioned in *al-Kashshaf*, I do not think is authentic. It was said: even if its authenticity is granted, what is meant is the negation of complete acceptance. It is also possible that what is meant by its raising it is its realization and strengthening, on the basis that the good word is faith, for there is no doubt that righteous deed establishes faith and realizes it by manifesting its effects, since through it the inward assent is known. It was also said: the subject is a pronoun referring to the good word, and the pronoun of the object refers to the righteous deed, meaning: the good word raises the righteous deed.

Abu Hayyan attributed this view to Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab. It was supported by the reading of 'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah, *wal-'amala al-salih* (and righteous deed) in the accusative, by the construction of *ishtighal* (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun). There is discussion about this, because the pronoun of *al-kalim* is not necessarily determined to be the subject. As for the meaning of the good word raising the righteous deed, it was said: it increases it in radiance and beauty.

Whoever explained the good word as the Oneness of God (*tawhid*) said: the meaning of that is making it accepted, for deed is not accepted except with *tawhid*. It was also said: the subject is a pronoun referring to Him, the Exalted, and the object pronoun refers to the deed. Ibn al-Mubarak related this from Qatadah, meaning: righteous deed is raised by Allah, the Exalted, and He accepts it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views to me. It was also said: the subject pronoun refers to the deed, and likewise the object pronoun, and the sentence is with an elided genitive (*hadhf mudaf*), meaning: righteous deed raises its doer and honours him. Abu Hayyan attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas, then said: it is permissible in my view that *al-'amal* (deed) be conjoined to *al-kalim*, and *yarfa'uhu* be a resumed statement of information, meaning: Allah, the Exalted, raises both of them. He made the pronoun singular because both share the ascent, and the pronoun may function like a demonstrative noun, so its form is singular while its meaning is dual, as if it were said: their ascent is not from themselves, but rather it is by the raising of Allah, the Exalted, of them both. He said this, and it is very contrary to the apparent meaning. Similar to it is what he attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and I do not think his attribution to him is sound. Even if it is granted, it is possible that he, may Allah be pleased with him, intended by his saying that righteous deed raises its doer and honours him, an explanation of what the verse indicates in general. What comes to my mind from the verse is what was related from Qatadah and chosen by Ibn 'Atiyyah.
