The exaltation of righteous deed being specified as the one that God Most High raises is said to be because of the hardship and difficulty in it, for it is the greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar). The apparent meaning of this is that deed is more noble than speech, and there is no dispute about this if by righteous deed is meant what includes the deed of the heart, such as belief (al-tasdiq). Perhaps the speech on it is like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143], and His words, Glorified is He: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [Al-Isra: 1]. The words of the Imam (al-Razi) are explicit that the good word, interpreted as remembrance (dhikr), is more noble than deed, since he made the ascent of the word by itself a proof of its preference over the deed that others raise. He said, regarding the reason for this: Speech is noble, for the distinction of man over every animal lies in speech and in action, in movement and in stillness, which man shares with others. When the noble person reaches the door of the king, he is not prevented, whereas one below him does not find the way except when he is summoned. What indicates this is that when the disbeliever utters the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah), he is safe from the punishment of both abodes if it is sincere, and he is safe in his self, his blood and his sanctity in this world if it is apparent; this is not the case with the deed of the limbs. Also, the heart is the origin, and what is in it does not appear except through the tongue, and what is in the tongue cannot be shown to be truthful except through action. So speech is closer to the heart than action, and therefore it is more noble than it. End of quotation. Yet there is something in it regarding the heart, so reflect.

﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾, that is, the evil plots (al-makrat al-sayyi'at), or the kinds of evil plots, with (al-sayyi'at) being an attribute of an omitted noun. It is not an object of yamkurun, because makara is intransitive. It is permitted that it be an object by implying yaqsidun (intend) or yaksibun (earn). According to the first, there is exaggeration in the severe threat against intending plotting, or it is an indication that their plotting has no effect. The relative pronoun is the subject, and the clause ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾ is its predicate, meaning: for them, because of their plotting, is a severe punishment that its measure cannot be gauged and which, compared to what they plot, is of no account.

According to what is related from Abu al-Aliyah, the verse concerns those who plotted against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Dar al-Nadwa, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30]. The present tense is for narrating a past situation. The placing of the demonstrative (ulaika) in place of their pronoun in His words, Glorified is He, ﴿And the plot of those﴾ is to signify the complete distinction of them by the evil and corruption they are upon, above all other corrupters, and their being well known for that. What is implied in it of distance is to alert to the far-reaching nature of their affair in transgression and the remoteness of their station in aggression. That is: and the plot of those well-known corrupters ﴿it will perish (huwa yabur)﴾, that is, it will be corrupted. The basic meaning of bawar is extreme slump or ruin, so it is here used for corruption, meaning lack of effect, because extreme slump leads to corruption, as it is said, "it slumped until it spoiled," or because the unsold goods slump generally due to their corruption, and because the one who is ruined is corrupt and has no effect.

﴿And the plot﴾ is the subject, its predicate being the clause ﴿it will perish﴾, and the fronting of the pronoun is for restriction or exclusivity, meaning: their plotting itself will be corrupted exclusively, not our plotting against them. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the predicate be the clause ﴿yabur﴾ with huwa as a separating pronoun (damir fasl). Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized this, saying that a separating pronoun cannot be followed by a verb, and no one that we know of has held this except Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani in his commentary on al-Idah, for he permitted in kana Zaydun huwa yaqumu that huwa be a separator, and this was refuted against him.

Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that huwa be an emphasis of the subject. The apparent meaning is what we have already mentioned. God Most High has destroyed those plotters after the destruction of their plot, when He expelled them from Mecca, killed them, and cast them into the well of Badr. Thus He gathered upon them their three plots, of which they had settled for only one against the Prophet (ﷺ), and He, Mighty and Majestic, fulfilled in their case His words, Glorified is He: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And evil plotting does not beset anyone except its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43].

As for the connection of the verse with what precedes it, according to what Shaykh al-Islam mentioned, it is an explanation of the state of the evil word and the evil deed and their people, after the explanation of the state of the good word and the righteous deed.

In al-Kashf: it is as though, when He, Glorified is He, restricted might and made it belong to Him, giving it to whom He wills, and guided to attaining that by which this sought goal is attained, He mentioned by way of digression the state of one who seeks might from other than God, Mighty and Majestic, and proceeded to humiliate one whom God Most High has honored above the Pleiades in rank, and that the consequence of that returned upon them, as evidence for that claim. This is the essence of what al-Tibi mentioned regarding the coherence (wajh al-intizam). It is related from Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Shahr ibn Hawshab that the verse concerns the people of showing off (ahl al-riya'), and it is connected with what is before it according to what is related from Shahr, where he said: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾ means they make a show (yuraun).

﴿And the plot of those, it will perish﴾: they are the people of showing off, their deed does not ascend. Al-Tibi said: the sentence according to this narration is conjoined to the sentence of the condition and the consequence, namely His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires might﴾ etc., so it is then necessary to observe the correspondence between the two parallel phrases and the antithesis between the two clauses as far as possible, by estimating in each of them what achieves the antithesis through the indication of what is mentioned in the first of what is left out in the second, and vice versa. End of quotation.

Its remoteness is not hidden. In any case, the present tense here is for continuous renewed duration (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi).

Allah created you from dust. This is another proof for the truth of resurrection (ba'th) and rising (nushur). That is, He created you at the beginning from dust, within the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, as a general creation. ﴿Then from a drop (nutfah)﴾, that is, then He created you from it as a detailed creation. ﴿Then He made you into pairs﴾, that is, into kinds, males and females, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾ [al-Shura: 50]. Ibn Abi Hatim related this from al-Suddi, and he and others related from Qatadah that he said: "He decreed among you marriage (zawjiyyah) and made some of you pairs for others."

﴿No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. The phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject, and "min" is extra (ziyadah). That is, "except while it is accompanied by His knowledge, exalted is He." The knownness of the agent (ma'lumiyyah al-fa'il) returns to the knownness of its states in detail, and among them is the state of what the female carried and what she delivered. So taking it in this sense is more eloquent in meaning and better in wording than taking it as referring to the object, meaning the carried and the delivered, because the object is omitted and left unstated, as al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated concerning Surah Ha Mim al-Sajdah. Making it a circumstantial clause from the carrying and delivering themselves is contrary to the apparent sense.

﴿Nor is any life lengthened (yu'ammar) of one who is lengthened﴾. That is, of anyone; that is, nor is anyone's lifespan extended. He is called "one who is lengthened" with regard to his first state, as in ﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36], and as in "whoever kills a slain man," according to what many have mentioned. This is to avoid the implication of obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil). It has been permitted to say that it is because ﴿yu'ammar﴾ is a present-tense verb, which requires that he not yet be lengthened, and there is no necessity to read it as past tense.

﴿Nor is any of his life shortened﴾. The pronoun refers to another lengthened one, similar to what Ibn Malik said in "I have a dirham and its half" (ʿindi dirham wa nisfuhu), meaning half of another dirham. It does no harm in this that it is possible the meaning is "like its half," because this is an example, and it is istikhdam or something similar to it. The grammarians al-Farra' and some of the Basran and Kufan grammarians (nahwiyyun) went to this view, and it is perhaps the most apparent. They explained the lengthened one as the one whose life has been increased, based on what is contrasted with it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor is it shortened﴾, etc. This is what led them to return the pronoun to a similar mentioned referent rather than to its very referent, since the one whose life is increased is not one whose life is diminished from his own life. It was said in response: Grant that the pronoun's referent is another lengthened one; has not the shortening of life been attributed to a lengthened one? And you have said it is the one whose life is increased. It was answered that the original is "and no one is lengthened except of a person," so he was called "lengthened" with regard to what he will become, and the pronoun returned according to the original from which it was changed. So the outcome is: "nor is the life of anyone shortened," that is, nor is he made short from the beginning of the matter. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "the narrowness of the mouth of the well."

Others said: The pronoun returns to the very same first lengthened one, and the lengthened one is the one for whom Allah, exalted is He, has decreed a lifespan, whether long or short. There is no obstacle to the lengthened one and the one whose life is shortened being one and the same person. The meaning of the shortening of his life is what passes from it and comes to an end. For example, his life is written as one hundred years, then beneath it is written: one day has passed, two days have passed, and so on until he arrives... This has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik, Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Suddi. It has also been said with the same meaning:

*Your life is breaths that are counted; whenever a breath of it passes, it has diminished by a part.*

It was also said: the increase and decrease are in one lifespan, with regard to different causes recorded in the Preserved Tablet, as occurs in the report: "Charity increases lifespan." So it is possible that a person is "lengthened," that is, has his life increased if he does a deed, and his life is shortened if he does not do it. This does not necessarily entail a change in the decree, because in His decree, exalted is He, it is also conditional. Yet what is in His eternal knowledge and His binding decree is not subject to erasure (mahw), as is known from the early generation (al-Salaf). For this reason it is permissible to supplicate for a long life.

Ka'b said: "If 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, had supplicated to Allah, exalted is He, his term would have been deferred." From this it is known that the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah, "this is a weak, rejected view which implies the doctrine of two terms (ajalayn), as the Mu'tazilah went to," is worthless. And strange is the statement of Ibn Kamal: "Careful reflection judges that the lengthened one, that is, the one for whom a long lifespan has been decreed, may or may not reach that age. So his life may increase beyond the first and be shortened beyond the second. Yet even so, this does not entail a change in the decree, because what is decreed for each person is the counted breaths, not the limited days or the extended years." Then he said: "Understand this wondrous secret." He wrote in the margin: "until the secret of the choice of restraining the self (habs al-nafs) is revealed to you and the wisdom of the correctness of his statement, peace and blessings be upon him, becomes clear: 'Indeed charity and kinship ties build up the abodes and increase lifespans.'" End of his quotation.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji criticized it, saying: this is among what no rational person relies upon, and no one has said it except some ignorant Indians, and moreover it contradicts what is in the authentic hadith which Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu al-Shaykh related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umm Habibah when she said: "O Allah, let me enjoy my two husbands, the Prophet (ﷺ) and my father Abu Sufyan, and my brother Mu'awiyah." He said: "You have asked Allah, exalted is He, for appointed terms (ajal madrubah) and counted days..." and the hadith continues. Al-Jalabi extended his refutation at length, though it was not necessary for him to do so. End of quotation.

Some of them said: It is possible that the one for whom a long life has been decreed does not reach what was decreed for him, by changing what was first decreed with another decree, and there is no restriction upon Allah, exalted is He. This is indicated by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith about the Tarawih prayer: "I feared that it would be made obligatory upon you," and his words (ﷺ) in the supplication of qunut: "Protect me from the evil of what You have decreed," and his fear from Allah, exalted is He, for thousands upon thousands of prayers and peace from the Hour when the wind is strong, along with his report that before it will come the emergence of the Mahdi, the Dajjal, the Beast, and the rising of the sun from the west, and other things that have not yet occurred. The most that follows from this is a change in the known (al-ma'lum), and it does not follow from it that knowledge changes, as has been explained in its proper place. On this basis there is no difficulty in the report, "Charity increases lifespan."

The matter of the benefit of supplication becomes clear, and what is related from some of them about denying the binding decree (al-qada' al-mubram) returns to this. I have seen a booklet by one of the virtuous scholars who spoke at length in it to strengthen this view and fortify its foundations. My own view is that what is in the eternal knowledge concerning things, as they are in reality, does not change, and it must occur as it is known. Otherwise reversal (inqilab) would follow, and what appears from it to the contrary, if it is authentic, must be interpreted.

As for the report, "Charity increases lifespan," it has been said that it is a single-chain report (khabar ahad), so it does not contradict certain matters (qat'iyyat). It has also been said that what is meant is that charity, and likewise other acts of obedience, increase what is the most important purpose of life, namely acquiring goodness, perfection and blessing, by which human souls are perfected and attain eternal happiness. Supplication has the same ruling as the other means, such as eating, drinking, and protecting oneself from extreme heat or cold, for example, so its benefit is like theirs. It has also been said that it is merely to manifest need and servitude. So let it be pondered.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to the one lengthened, and the shortening refers to another. That is, nor is the lifespan of the one lengthened shortened for another, by giving to another a lifespan that is shorter than his. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the one shortened in his lifespan, and although this is not explicitly stated, it is understood in the sense of what was mentioned, as is said:

*And by their opposites things are made clear.*

So it refers to what is known from the context, that is, nor is the lifespan of the one whose life is shortened shortened further by making it short.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and 'Isa read "wa la yanqusu" with the active voice, and its subject is either the pronoun of the one lengthened or "'umrihi," and "min" is extra in the subject. Although the verb is transitive, it is permissible for its subject to be the pronoun of Allah, exalted is He. Al-A'raj read "min 'umrihi" with a sukun on the mim.

﴿Except in a Book﴾. According to Ibn 'Abbas, it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It is also permissible that it means the record (sahifah) of the human being. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Hudhayfah ibn Usayd al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angel enters upon the drop after it settles in the womb, forty or forty-five nights later, and says: 'O Lord, is he wretched or happy? Male or female?' Allah, exalted is He, says, and he writes. Then he writes his deed, his provision, his term, his trace, and his affliction. Then the record is folded up, and nothing is added to it or subtracted from it."

It is also permissible that it means the knowledge of Allah, mighty and majestic. It was mentioned in the connection of the verses (rabt al-ayat) that His words, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ etc., are intended to show complete power; His words, ﴿And no female carries or gives birth﴾ [Fussilat: 47] etc., show comprehensive knowledge; and His words, mighty and majestic, ﴿Nor is any life lengthened of one who is lengthened﴾ etc., establish qada' and qadar. The meaning is: "and no one of you is lengthened," addressing the individuals of the human species. This first aspect of the meanings of ﴿and no one is lengthened﴾ etc. is supported by this.

﴿Indeed that﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of the creation and what follows it, even though it bewilders minds and understandings, ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, because He, exalted is He, is free from needing causes. Likewise, then, is resurrection and rising.

[p. 178]

﴿And the two seas are not alike.﴾ This one ﴿is sweet﴾, pleasant, ﴿fresh﴾, quenching thirst and removing it. Al-Raghib said: al-furat is sweet water, used for both the singular and the plural. Perhaps the description in this sense is of varieties: ﴿intensely black﴾ and ﴿bright yellow﴾.

﴿Palatable is its drink﴾: easy to swallow, because it is free of what the soul dislikes. Isa read sayyigh (سَيِّغٌ) like mayyit, with doubling, and this is also reported from Abu Amr and Asim. Isa also read saygh (سَيْغٌ) like mayt, without doubling.

﴿And this is salty﴾: its taste is changed in the well-known way. Abu Nahik and Talha read malih (مَلِحٌ) with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam. Abu al-Fath al-Razi said: this is an irregular dialect form. It is also permitted that it is a shortened form of mali (مالِحٌ) for lightness, and this is based on the occurrence of mali, although the correct view is that it occurs rarely, and it is not a poor dialect as has been said. Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) distinguished between malih (المَلِحُ) and mali (المالِحُ): malih is water that has the known taste from its original creation, like the water of the sea; mali is water into which salt has been put so that its taste has changed, and it is said only as mali, and I have not seen it used otherwise. Some said: mali does not occur at all in this sense, but this is not a fine view.

﴿Bitter﴾: intensely salty and hot, from their saying ajij al-nar (أجِيجُ النّارِ, the crackling of fire) and ajjatuha (أجَّتُها, its blazing). From here it is said that it is the water that burns with its saltiness. This is a parable struck for the believer and the disbeliever.

Allah's statement: ﴿and from each﴾, that is, from each one of the two, ﴿you eat fresh flesh﴾, that is, tender and new, which is fish according to what is narrated from al-Suddi. It was said: birds and fish. Many preferred the first view. Calling fish "flesh," though it is an animal, has been said to be an allusion to the restriction of benefit from it to eating. Describing it as fresh indicates its delicacy and draws attention to hastening to eat it, lest decay hasten to it, as is indicated by making each of the two seas the source of its eating.

Malik and al-Thawri used the verse, since fish is called flesh in it, as evidence that one who swears not to eat meat and then eats fish breaks his oath. Others said he does not break it, because oaths are based on custom, and in custom fish is not called meat. For this reason, one who swears not to ride a beast and then rides a disbeliever does not break it, although Allah the Exalted called it a beast in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in Allah's sight are those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 55]. In my view, it is not far-fetched that by ﴿flesh﴾ is meant the flesh of fish. The claim that the allusion is to the restriction of benefit from fish to eating, I do not think is sound.

﴿And you extract﴾: its apparent meaning is that from each of them you extract ﴿ornaments which you wear﴾. The ornament extracted from the salt sea is pearls and coral, and men and women wear these, though the manner of wearing differs. Or it is said: he expressed the wearing of their women as wearing by them, because they are of them or because their wearing is for their sake. We do not know of an ornament extracted from fresh water. The attribution of what belongs to some to the whole does not clearly apply here, as it was considered in His saying: ﴿From them come out the pearl and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22]. As for the fact that some rocks in the courses of torrents are broken and found to contain diamonds, which is an ornament worn, if this is correct, it is not useful to consider it here, since it does not clearly involve extracting an ornament from fresh water. It was also said: it is not far that the ornament extracted from that is the bones of fish, from which hilts of swords and daggers are made, for example, so they are carried and adorned with. There is much to say about this, especially if the ornament is like jewelry, meaning what is adorned with metal or stone.

al-Khafaji said: there is no objection to pearls coming out of fresh waters, even though we have not seen it. This is far-fetched, and its distance is not hidden.

Some eminent scholars, to escape the debate, held that what is meant is that you extract from the salt sea alone an ornament which you wear, and al-Suddi's statement suggests this. It admits three aspects:

The first: it is a digression (istitrad) in describing the two seas and the blessings and benefits in them.

The second: it is a completion and perfection of the parable (tamthil), to show the superiority of the thing compared (al-mushabbah bihi) over the thing being compared (al-mushabbah). It is not, as al-Tibi claimed, a development of the metaphor (tarshih al-isti'ara) at all; rather it is a correction (istidrak) to the claim of sharing between the thing compared and the thing compared to, which necessarily implies that the thing compared is stronger. This correction is specific to the salt water. Its clarification is that He compared the believer and the disbeliever to the two seas, then preferred the bitter water over the disbeliever in that it shares with the fresh water in benefits, while the disbeliever is empty of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74], then He said: ﴿And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split and water issues from them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74].

The third: it is part of the parable, in the sense that although the two seas share some benefits, they differ in what is the essential purpose, because one of them has been mixed with what has not left it in the purity of its natural state. So it is with the believer and the disbeliever. Although they may agree in some noble qualities such as courage and generosity, they differ in what is fundamental, since one of them remains upon the original nature and the other does not. Thus the clause ﴿And from each﴾ etc. is a circumstantial clause (hali).

In my view the best of the three aspects is the middle one. In every case, the answer is obtained to the question of how the mention of the benefits of the salt sea fits when the disbeliever has been compared to it. Abu Hayyan said: the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾ etc., is to explain what every intelligent person may use as evidence that no idol has any part in it.

Imam (al-Razi) said: the more apparent view is that it is evidence of the perfect power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. What we mentioned first, that it is a parable for the believer and the disbeliever, is the most famous in transmission and in understanding, and it contains of the excellences of eloquence what it contains.

﴿And you see the ships﴾, the boats, ﴿in it﴾, that is, in each of them. Consider whether it is good to return the pronoun to the salt sea, since the mind is drawn to it from His statement: ﴿And you extract an ornament which you wear﴾, based on the fact that extraction from it alone is well known. The matter of ships in it is greater than their matter in the fresh sea. For this reason the verse limited seeing the ships in it to the state which Allah mentioned. The pronoun of address is singular, although it is plural in what precedes and what follows, because the address is to everyone who is capable of seeing, not only to those who benefit from the two seas.

﴿Ploughing﴾ (mawakhir): cutting through the water, driving them forward and backward with one wind. The makhr is cutting. Al-Raghib said: it is said makharat al-safinah makhran wa-mukhuran when the ship cut the water with its prow. In al-Kashshaf it is said: makharat al-safinah al-ma' (the ship ploughed the water). It is said of clouds: banat makhr, because they plough the air. The safn from which safinah (ship) is derived is close to makhr, because they scrape the water as if peeling it, just as they plough it. It was also said that makhr is the sound of ships running. In Surat (al-Nahl) came: ﴿And you see the ships ploughing therein﴾ [al-Nahl: 14], with mawakhir placed first and fihi (in it) placed later. Here it is reversed. It was said, as its reason, that fihi here is connected to tara (you see), and there it is connected to mawakhir, and this does not close the question.

What appears to me regarding this is that the verse of al-Nahl was brought to enumerate blessings, as its preceding and following verses indicate, and the verse is followed by His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34; al-Nahl: 18]. So what was more important there was to put first what is a blessing, which is the ploughing of ships through water, unlike here, where it was brought as a digression or as a completion of the parable, as you have known just now. So fihi was placed first in it, to indicate that the purpose in itself is not that. It seems that concern with what is there required that in that verse it be said wa-li-tabtaghu (and that you may seek), with the waw, and the difference here required omitting the waw in His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾, that is, of the bounty of Allah the Exalted, by the movement in it. He, glory be to Him, although no mention of Him occurred in the verse, mention of Him occurred before it, and even if it had not, it would not be confusing, since the meaning points to Him, exalted is His majesty.

The lam is connected to mawakhir. It is also permitted that it is connected to a omitted verb indicated by the verbs mentioned, such as sakhkhar al-bahrayn (He subjected the two seas) and hayya'ahuma (He prepared them), or: He did that ﴿that you may seek of His bounty, and that perhaps you may be grateful﴾, meaning: you know His rights, so you stand in obedience to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and in His unity, glory be to Him.

The la'alla (لَعَلَّ, perhaps) indicates cause, according to what a group of eminent scholars held, and we have already mentioned this. Many said: it is for hope (tarajji), and since that is impossible for Allah, the intended meaning is that the blessings mentioned require gratitude, as if everyone hopes for it from the one who bestowed them on him. This is a parable which returns to His command to the addressees to be grateful.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 13:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, by the increase of one and the decrease of the other, by adding some parts of each of them to the other. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿causes to enter﴾. The difference between them in form (ṣīghah) is because the entering of one into the other is renewed from time to time, whereas the subjecting of the two luminaries is a matter in which there is no multiplicity; what is multiple and renewed are its effects. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿each﴾ of the sun and the moon ﴿runs﴾, meaning in accordance with its motion along its daily orbits, which are multiple according to the number of the days of the year, or in accordance with its two particular motions, the first from west to east and the compelled one from east to west, running continuously. ﴿For a term appointed﴾, which God, exalted is He, determined for their running, and it is the Day of Resurrection, as narrated from al-Hasan.

It has been said that their running is an expression for their two particular motions, and the appointed term is an expression for the totality of the duration of their two revolutions, or its endpoint, which for the sun is one year and for the moon one month. The discussion of this has already been detailed earlier.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the doer of the mentioned actions, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the utmost grandeur. It is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it are successive predicates, meaning: that is the One of exalted station who originated these wondrous creations, ﴿God, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion﴾. In it there is an indication that His, exalted is He, originating those wonders is what necessitates the establishment of those predicates for Him, exalted is He.

In al-Kashshaf: "It is permissible in terms of i'rab to make the name of God, exalted is He, a qualifier (ṣifah) of the demonstrative, or an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān), and 'your Lord' a predicate, were it not that the meaning rejects it." End of quote.

In al-Kashf it is said: "There is scrutiny in this, because the noble name is treated as a proper noun (ʿalam), so it is not permissible for it to be a qualifier of a demonstrative at all, neither verbally nor in meaning. It seems he assumed this on the supposition of the absence of predominance. As for the meaning rejecting it on the supposition of permitting it as a qualifier, it has been said that the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, is singular in divinity, not that the one singular in divinity is your Lord, because the polytheists did not acknowledge an absolutely singular one. As for the appositive, it has been said that it gives the impression of association, do you not see that when you say 'that man is your master in my view,' there is a kind of association, since 'that' is an ambiguous noun. It seems he meant that the appositive, where the mind goes to something else and admits association, is appropriate but not in such a context."

Al-Tibi stated that the demonstrative refers to what has preceded, to indicate that what follows is worthy by virtue of the preceding attributes; and if it were a qualifier or an appositive, the referent would be what follows. This is good in the first case but not the second, unless his words "or an appositive" are an indication of the view that makes the noun that follows the ambiguous demonstrative a non-qualifier, so that its ruling then becomes that of a qualifier. And after it became clear that the context is for indicating what precedes, the demonstrative may be used for other purposes. End of quote.

Abu Hayyan prevented the validity of being a qualifier for a proper noun. Then he said: the rejection of the meaning does not clearly show that. It is possible that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to Him belongs the dominion﴾ is a new independent sentence set in contrast to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a qunṭīr﴾, and that this confirms what came before of the singularity in divinity and lordship and serves as evidence for it, since its sum is that all dominion and disposal in beginning and end belongs to Him, exalted is He, and nothing of it belongs to others besides Him, glorified is He. For this reason it has been said that there is an implicit logical syllogism in it.

It is also permitted that it confirms His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God created you﴾ etc., and His saying, ﴿He causes to enter﴾ etc. Then the sentence ﴿those you invoke﴾ etc. is either also a resumptive sentence, conjoined to the sentence ﴿to Him belongs the dominion﴾, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun resting in the adverbial phrase, namely "to Him." On the first view it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿that God﴾ etc., or also a circumstantial clause.

The qiṭmīr, according to what Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Mujahid, is the thin wrapping of the date-stone, which is the thin white skin between the date and the stone, and this is the well-known meaning. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated that it is the cap that is on the top of the date. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatada that it is the skin on the top of the stone, which is what lies between the cap and the stone. Al-Raghib said: it is the trace on the back of the stone. It has also been said that it is the peel of garlic. Whatever it is, it is a metaphor for a base and trivial thing. The poet said:

"Your father mends his sandal, patched, what the poor man owns of qiṭmīr."

ʿĪsā, Sallām and Yaʿqūb read (yadʿūna) with the yā' of the third person.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 14:

﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a sentence beginning a new clause) that confirms what precedes it and reveals the clear state of those they call upon: that they are inanimate objects, and hearing is not part of their nature. This is the case if the discourse is with the idol-worshippers. It is possible that the discourse is with them, with the worshippers of angels, with the worshippers of Jesus, and with others among those brought near (to God). Non-hearing in that case is either because the one worshipped is not of the kind that hears, as with idols, or because it is occupied with a preoccupying matter and is at a great distance from its worshipper, as with Jesus, peace be upon him. This was narrated from al-Balkhi. Or it is because God, Mighty and Majestic, has protected its hearing from such a supplication reaching it, because of its extreme ugliness and its heaviness on the hearing of one who is in the utmost servitude to God, glory be to Him. Therefore it is not objected that the angels, peace be upon them, do hear, and they are in the heavens, as was reported in some traditions regarding the supplication of believers to their Lord, glory be to Him. As for placing those possessed of holy souls in the same category as the angels, peace be upon them, with regard to hearing while they are in their abodes of bliss, I have a reservation about it. Indeed, regarding the hearing of each of the angels, peace be upon them, while they are in the heavens, and of those possessed of holy souls while they are in their abodes of bliss, of the call of one who calls them without believing in their divinity, I also have a reservation, since I have not found an authentic textual proof for that. Reason permits it, but mere permissibility is not enough to affirm it.

﴿And even if they heard﴾, by way of supposition and assumption, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, because they have not been granted the faculty of speech, and hearing does not entail that. Thus the meaning of "response" is response by speech. It is also permissible that it means response by action, i.e., even if they heard, they would not benefit you, due to their total inability to act. This is the case if those called upon are idols. As for if they are the angels, peace be upon them, or others like them among those brought near, then the lack of verbal response is because their calling upon them is on the basis that they are supposed to be gods, while they are far removed from divinity, so how would they respond to one who claims that concerning them, and there is in that what there is of accusation. The lack of practical response may also be for this reason, and it may be because benefiting one who calls upon them is not among their duties. It was also said that they regard that as a deficiency in servitude and submission to God, Mighty and Majestic. It is also permissible that this be a reason for the first as well, so reflect.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association﴾. Even less will they respond to you when you call upon them. "Shirk" (association) is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your associating them (with God) and your worshipping them. That will happen either by God enabling the idols to speak, so they say to them, "You did not used to worship us," or by their condition showing forth like the blaze of the night-fires of the villages, with knowledge of what indicates that. The language of the state is more eloquent than the language of speech. Of this kind is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

I stood at a ruined abode of Mayya, speaking,
its traces address me, and I address it,
and I water it until it nearly
—from what I pour out—its stones and its playgrounds speak to me.

If those called upon are the angels or the like, then the matter of speech is evident. God, exalted is He, has related the words of the angels to the polytheists in the preceding surah with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And on the day when He will gather them all, He will say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?" They will say, "Glory be to You, You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."﴾ [Saba': 40–41].

﴿And none can inform you like the All-Knowing﴾. That is, no informant informs you of the matter like an informant who is All-Knowing and has informed you of it, meaning by it God Himself, as was narrated from Qatada and others, for He, glory be to Him, is the Knower of the essence of matters. This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is also permissible that it not be restricted to him, meaning: no informant, O listener, whoever you are, informs you of the like of the Knowing, the Aware, from whom nothing is hidden in the earth or in the heavens. The purpose is to affirm what He, glory be to Him, has informed about the condition of their deities and to negate what they claim for them of divinity.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that this is part of the mention of the idols, as if it was said: "And none informs you like one who informs you about himself, and they have informed about themselves that they are not gods." In this there is what there is of remoteness.

O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah, in yourselves and in what befalls you of important matters or a pressing calamity. The definite article in "al-fuqara'" (the poor) is either for the category (lil-jins) or for comprehensiveness (lil-istighraq), since there is no prior reference. It is also defined for emphasis on their poverty, as if, because of the abundance of their need and the intensity of their dependence, they alone are "the poor" absolutely, and the need of all other creatures in comparison to their poverty is like nonexistence. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa': 28]. The jinn are not an objection, for they do not need food, clothing and the like as man does, and their weakness is not like his weakness; so there is no need to include them among "mankind" by way of taghlib (predominance). It has also been said that this does no harm, since the address is to those among mankind who display strength and obstinacy. As for the view that the restriction is relative with respect to Him, exalted is He, its defect is not hidden.

The author of al-Fara'id said: The proper view, and Allah knows best, is that the intended meaning is mankind and others, following the method of giving precedence to the present over the absent and to those possessing knowledge over others. But this is very far-fetched.

The scholar al-Tibi said: What the sublime composition requires is that the definiteness in "an-nas" (mankind) be taken as referring to a specific group (lil-'ahd), and in "al-fuqara'" as for the category (lil-jins), because the addressees are those who were addressed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion﴾, meaning: that worshipped One is the One described with the attributes of majesty, not those you invoke besides Him, while you are the creatures most in need of Him, glorified and exalted is He. This is not devoid of beauty.

﴿And Allah is the Rich (al-Ghani)﴾ free of all need of everything, none other than Him, ﴿the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾, the Bestower of blessings upon all existing things, deserving of praise for His bounty, glorified is He. Its original form is "al-mahmud", but it is intended in this sense by way of kinaya (metonymy), so that it corresponds to the mention of it after their poverty, since the Rich does not benefit the poor unless He is generous and bountiful, and one such is deserving of praise. This is like a completion of what precedes it, as in the verse of Ka'b al-Ghanawi:

Forbearing, when forbearance adorns its people, and together with forbearance he is awe-inspiring in the eye of the enemy.

Included in the generality of "the One free of need" are the addressees and their worship. In al-Tibi's statement there is a whiff of restriction, where he said: "I have not heard it transmitted that He, glorified is He, is free of you and of your worship, because He, exalted is He, is praiseworthy, having servants who praise Him even if you do not praise Him." The better course is generality.

As for what is related concerning the occasion of revelation, that when the Prophet ﷺ supplicated much and the disbelievers persisted much, they said, "Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, is in need of our worship," and so this was revealed, it does not necessitate any restriction in the verse, as is not hidden.

﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾: that is, if He, glorified is He, wills to remove you, O people, and to bring a new creation that will take your place, ﴿and bring a new creation﴾: a world other than mankind that you do not know. This is if the address is general. Or, "If He wills, He will take you away, O polytheists, or O Arabs, and bring a new creation," who are not in your condition but remain steadfast in His obedience and His oneness. This is if the address is specific. The interpretation of "new" as you have heard has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. In either case, the sentence serves to affirm His self-sufficiency, mighty and majestic is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 17:

﴿And that﴾ means: that which has been mentioned, namely their being removed and the bringing of a new creation, ﴿for Allah is not difficult﴾ means: not hard. For His command, when He wills something, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.

Although among people there is the prevalence of the present over the absent and of those possessing knowledge over others, and the address here was in that style, and we have said that the verse indicates that what Allah, glorified is He, brings into being from the world is more wondrous, there arises, on the apparent reading, the statement of Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali): "It is not within possibility that something more wondrous than what has existed should come to be."

It is answered that this, on the assumption of its occurrence, falls within the scope of what has existed, and it is, together with this world, like some parts of this world together with others. Or it is answered that the wondrousness that is perceived is in one sense, and the wondrousness in the words of Hujjat al-Islam is in another sense. So reflect.

[p. 185]

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾: that is, no sinful soul shall bear the sin of another soul. Rather, every soul bears its own burden. There is no contradiction between this and His, the Exalted's, saying in Surah al-'Ankabut: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. That verse concerns the misguided who lead others astray: they bear the sin of leading others astray along with the sin of their own error. All of these are their own sins, and none of them contains any part of the sins of others. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿along with their burdens﴾ does not contradict this, because what is meant by "their burdens" is what they committed directly, and what is meant by "along with them" is what they caused through incitement and causation. Thus it applies to the misleaders in one respect and to the others in another respect.

﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load﴾: that is, a soul weighed down by sins calls to its load, the burden that weighs it down and its sin that overwhelms it, so that some of it may be carried and lightened for it. It was said: that is, to the bearing of its load. ﴿None of it will be carried﴾: it will not be answered by bearing any part of it. The apparent meaning is that ﴿And no bearer of burdens﴾ and what follows is a negation of voluntary bearing, out of the generosity of the bearer's own soul, in refutation of the words of the misleaders: ﴿And let us bear your sins﴾. This is supported by the occasion of revelation, for it is related that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said to a group of believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ, and upon me is your burden," and so this was revealed.

This is a negation of bearing after a request from the bearer, which is more general, whether it be by choice or by compulsion. If no one is compelled to bear after being asked and sought for help, then it is known by a stronger argument that there is no compulsion without that. Therefore the negation encompasses all kinds of bearing. Likewise, the bearer may or may not be one who bears a burden of his own. The generality came from not mentioning the one called upon explicitly. It may be said, despite this, that the first clause negates the bearing of the whole burden such that the one bearing it is stripped of it, and the second negates the lightening of it. Thus there is no contradiction between the meanings of the two clauses, as is not hidden.

It was said regarding the difference between them: the first is a negation of bearing by compulsion, and the second is a negation of it by choice. This was objected to: on this view, the appropriate phrasing would be "and no one shall be burdened with the burden of another," and "if one heavily laden calls someone to its load, he will not bear any of it." Also, the right order would be to address the negation of compulsion after the negation of choice.

It was said: the first clause, just as it indicates that one weighed down by sins will not have anyone bear any of his sins, indicates the perfection of His justice, the Exalted. The second clause indicates that there is also no one to seek help from the terror of that Day. These are the two intended meanings of the two verses. [p. 186] Thus the difference is considered in light of this. Perhaps what we mentioned first is better.

Some eminent scholars mentioned three questions regarding the first clause. Concerning the last two of them, he said: "I have not seen anyone who noticed them," and he answered each of them.

The first: the non-bearing of one party's burden by another is general, concerning a sinful soul and a non-sinful soul. Why, then, was it restricted to the sinful soul, when stating the generality explicitly is more complete in justice, more eloquent in good tidings, and more concise in wording? That would be to say: "And no soul shall bear the burden of another"? Its answer: the discourse concerns the people of burdens who are being punished, to explain that their punishment is only for what they themselves committed of burdens, not for what others committed.

The second: the meaning of "wizr" (burden) is the bearing of a burden, not mere bearing in general, according to what is in al-Nihayah al-Athiriyyah, where he said: "It is said: wazara yazIru, so he is a wazir (bearer) when he carries what weighs down his back, from heavy things, and from sins." How then is the mention of "wizr" with "yazir" correct? Its answer: it is from the rhetorical device of tajrid (abstraction, where a term is used in a derived sense to strengthen the meaning).

The third: "wazirah" (bearer) is understood from "tazir," just as "darib" (striker) is understood from "yadrib," for example. So what is the benefit of mentioning it? Its answer: when it is said "a striker struck Zayd," what is understood from "struck" is an entity in which the striking, an event, subsists, through the relation of this act to that entity. When something is expressed by a term that carries a descriptive sense, and a verbal meaning is attached to it in the form fa'ala or otherwise, it is understood in the usage of the language that the thing is characterized by that attribute at the time the meaning is attached to it, not because of it, as one of the eminent commentators on al-Kashshaf verified. Therefore the meaning of "darib" in the example must be one characterized by a striking prior to the attachment of "darab" to it. The same is said regarding ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

This is a glorious benefit, and its glory is increased by the derivation of generality when the active participle is placed indefinitely within a negation. By this, the statement of al-Taftazani falls away, that mentioning the agent of the verb by the form of its active participle indefinitely is of very little use at all. End.

You know that from the two clauses together, the generality mentioned in the first question is derived, and in the specific content of these two clauses and their being mentioned together there is benefit that is not hidden. In al-Qamus: "wazarahu, like wa'adahu, wizran with a kasra, means he carried it." In al-Kashshaf: "wazara al-shay' means he carried it," and similarly in al-Bahr. According to this, there is no need for tajrid, so do not overlook this.

The original meaning of carrying is what is on the back of something heavy, and it is then borrowed for abstract meanings of sins and offenses. Abu al-Sammal, on the authority of Talhah and Ibrahim, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read ﴿lā taḥmil﴾ with a fatha on the upper tā' and a kasra on the mīm. This reading requires that "shay'" be in the accusative as the direct object of "tahmil," and its subject is a pronoun referring to the omitted object of "tad'u." That is: and if one heavily laden calls a soul to its load, it will not bear any of it. ﴿Even if he were of kin﴾: that is, the one called, understood from the calling, [would be] a relative of the caller. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the subject of "kana" is the pronoun of the caller, that is, even if the caller were a relative of the one called. The former is better, because the caller is the very one who is heavily laden, so the apparent reference of the pronoun is to him, and its feminine form matches him.

As for Abu Hayyan's statement that the pronoun was mentioned by consideration of meaning, because His saying "heavily laden" does not refer only to the feminine sense, but to every person, so it is as if it were said: "and if a heavily laden person calls," it is not hidden what is problematic in it.

It was read as ﴿dhū qurbā﴾ with a damma (dhu qurba) in "kana," and it was given the same analysis: "kana" is also defective (incomplete), and "dhu qurba" is its subject, with an omitted predicate, that is: even if a relative were called. It was permitted that it be complete (taamma), but it was objected that the sublime composition does not harmonize with it, because the conditional clause serves as a completion and emphasis on the point that there is no help at all. This would imply that the meaning is: if the heavily laden calls someone to its load, he will not answer its call even if a relative were called. But if we said: if the heavily laden calls someone to its load, the one called will not bear anything of it, even if a relative were present, that excellence would not be achieved. Taking into account that the relative is the one called, by the context or by estimating "fa-da'athu," as Abu Hayyan did, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the coherence of the composition escapes him.

﴿You only warn﴾ and so on: a resumptive clause brought to explain who is admonished by what has been mentioned. That is: you only warn with these warnings and the like ﴿those who fear their Lord unseen﴾: that is, they fear Him, the Exalted, being absent from His punishment, glorified is He, or absent from people in their private moments, or they fear the punishment of their Lord while it is unseen by them. The prepositional phrase is then in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to either the subject or the object.

[p. 187 not included; the passage continues:]

﴿And establish the prayer﴾: that is, they observe it as it should be, and they made it a standing pillar and a raised banner. That is: your warning and admonition benefit only these people of your nation, and not those beyond them from among the rebellious and obstinate. The reason for the difference between the two verbs is known from what has passed in His saying: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾, so recall what is in the old covenant.

﴿And whoever purifies himself﴾: he cleanses himself from the filth of sins and disobedience by being affected by these warnings. ﴿Then he purifies himself only for himself﴾: because its benefit is confined to himself, just as whoever is defiled by them is defiled only to his own harm. Purification encompasses both fear and the establishment of prayer, so this is an affirmation and an exhortation to both.

Al-'Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wa-man yazzakka fa-innama yazzakka﴾ with the yā' at the beginning and a shadda on the zāy in both. Both are present-tense forms; their origin is ﴿wa-man yatazakka fa-innama yatazakka﴾, and the tā' was assimilated into the zāy, as it was assimilated in ﴿yadhdhakkarūn﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Talhah read ﴿wa-man izzakka﴾ with the tā' assimilated into the zāy and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) brought at the beginning. Talhah also read ﴿fa-innama tazzakka﴾ with the tā' assimilated into the zāy.

﴿And to Allah is the return﴾: not to anyone other than Him, whether independently or in partnership, so He will reward them for their purification with the best of rewards.

﴿Nor are the blind and the seeing alike﴾ is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾. The blind and the seeing are two parables (*mathalan*, parables or similitudes) for the disbeliever and the believer, as Qatada, al-Suddi (Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi) and others have said. It was also said: they are two parables for the idol and for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In that case, it is part of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion﴾, and the meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, is not equal to what you worship.

ولا الظُّلُمَاتُ ولا النُّورُ — that is, neither falsehood nor truth. ﴿Nor the darkness and nor the light.﴾ ولا الظِّلُّ ولا الحَرُورُ — nor the shade nor the scorching heat. That is: neither reward nor punishment. It has also been said: neither Paradise nor Hellfire.

Al-Harur (الحَرُورُ) is an intensive form (fa'ul) derived from al-harr (heat). It has been related from al-Farra' that it is applied to intense heat, whether by night or by day. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is the intensity of the heat of the sun. In al-Kashshaf, al-Harur is the samum (scorching wind), except that the samum occurs by day, whereas al-harur occurs by night and by day. It has also been said that it occurs only by night.

ولا الظُّلُمَاتُ ولا النُّورُ — that is, neither falsehood nor truth. ﴿Nor the darkness and nor the light.﴾ ولا الظِّلُّ ولا الحَرُورُ — nor the shade nor the scorching heat. That is: neither reward nor punishment. It has also been said: neither Paradise nor Hellfire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 22:

﴿And the living and the dead are not alike.﴾ This is another parable for the believers who entered the religion after the mission (al-ba'tha), and the disbelievers who persisted and were arrogant. The definite article here, as al-Tibi said, is for the known (li-l-'ahd); and it was said that it is for the learned and the ignorant. Al-Tha'alibi made the blind and the seeing two parables for these two groups, but that is not the right view.

﴿Indeed, Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, that is, He causes him to hear and makes him perceive sounds. Al-Khafaji and others said: perhaps the verse implies that what is meant is that He makes hear whom He wills with the hearing of reflection and acceptance of His signs, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾. This is a reinforcement of the parable of the persistent disbelievers as dead, and an intensification of the despair of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, from their faith. The particle bi- (ب) is extra, for emphasis, meaning: "and you are not one who makes hear." The hearing meant here is the same as what was meant in the previous clause. The meaning of hearing that is well known does not contradict what is related in the hadith of the well (al-qalib), because what is intended is the negation of making hear by way of habit; and what is in the hadith is of the category of ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17]. Some scholars have gone this way, and the discussion of this has already passed, so do not be heedless.

How elegant is the arrangement of these parables. He first likened the believer and the disbeliever to the two seas, and gave preference to the salty bitter sea over the disbeliever for its lack of benefit. Then he likened them to the blind and the seeing, followed by darknesses and light, shade and scorching heat. He did not suffice with the loss of the light of sight until he added to it the loss of what sustains it of external light, and joined to it the result of that blindness and loss. Thus there is an ascent from the first comparison to this one. Then [he likened them] to the living and the dead, in a second ascent. And he followed his saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾.

Al-Tibi mentioned that the omission of the emphatic la (لا) from the second [member] is because it serves as a preparation for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾. For this reason he repeated (وما يستوي). As for its mention in the two parables after it, it is because they are intended in themselves, since in them are two parables for truth and falsehood and what they lead to of reward and punishment, rather than the believer and the disbeliever as in other places. It has been taken that [the la] is extra for emphasis, since the intended meaning is not that the darknesses in themselves are not equal, but rather they differ: one darkness is, for instance, more intense than another. The same is said of what follows: rather, the intended meaning is that the darknesses are not equal to the light, the shade is not equal to the scorching heat, and the living are not equal to the dead.

Ibn 'Atiyya claimed that the entry of la is with the intention of repetition, as if it were said: "nor the darknesses and the light, and nor the light and the darknesses," and thus by mentioning the first items he dispensed with the second, and the stated speech indicates what is omitted. But the view that they are extra for emphasis of the negation makes unnecessary the consideration of this deletion, which has no benefit.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: la was repeated in what was repeated to emphasize the incompatibility. The darknesses are incompatible with the light and opposed to it; and the shade and the scorching heat are likewise, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold. This differs from the blind and the seeing, for one and the same person may be seeing and then blindness befalls him, so there is no incompatibility except in terms of the attribute. As for the living and the dead, although in them, like the blind and the seeing, one and the same body may be living and then death befalls it, yet the incompatibility between the living and the dead is more complete than the incompatibility between the blind and the seeing, for they may share in perceiving some things, whereas the living and the dead do not, and how could they, since the dead differs from the living in reality, as has been made clear in divine wisdom.

It was said: [la] was not repeated. It was said: it was repeated afterwards because the addressee at the beginning of the speech does not fall short in understanding the intended meaning. It was said: it was repeated in all except the last, because if it were said "and the blind and the seeing are not alike, nor the darknesses and the light," for instance, it would be wrongly assumed that the negation of equality applies between the whole group of the blind and the seeing and the whole group of the darknesses and the light. In the last, [repetition is for] attention. And the entry of la upon the two opposites is to remind of the negation of equality.

The blind is placed before the seeing, although the seeing is more honourable, because it is an indication of the disbeliever, who existed before the mission and the call to faith. For a similar reason the darknesses are placed before the light, for falsehood existed and then the truth crushed it by His mission, upon him be blessings and peace. The scorching heat was not placed before the shade, so as not to follow the pattern of what came before of placing the less honourable first; rather the shade was placed first, in consideration of its suitability to blindness and darkness in some respect, or because mercy precedes [wrath], together with what that involves of observing the rhyme (fasila).

The living are placed before the dead, and the order was not reversed to accord with the first two in placing the less honourable first, because the living are an indication of the believers after the call, and the dead are an indication of those who persist in disbelief after it. That is why it was said afterwards: ﴿Indeed, Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, etc. The existence of those persisting in the attribute of persistence comes after the existence of the believers. It was said that what was placed first, except in the last, is because it is a privation, and privation has the rank of priority; and in the last, because the dead are meant as those who lack life after having possessed it, as is suggested by the following of it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you cannot make hear those who are in the graves﴾. So life, although it is existential, has priority of rank as well. It was also said that placing the less honourable first, along with the implication that it is less honourable, is to indicate that the placing is a matter of form which does not diminish the honour of the more honourable, as the poet said:

So fire is overtopped by smoke, and perhaps dust rises above the turbans of horsemen.

The plural of darknesses with the singular of light is because the kinds of falsehood are many while the truth is one. It was also said: because darkness may be multiple, existing in places separated by light; and light in this world, though it may be multiple, is one behind the place of its multiplicity. The living and the dead are plural in their regular form, because the things likened to them are many. The blind and the seeing were not pluralised for this reason, because the aim is the genus, and the singular is more apt in it; moreover, in the plural form "al-buṣara" there would be a loss of observing the rhyme, which is on sound taste preferable to "al-basir." So reflect on all of this, and Allah the Exalted knows best the secrets of His Book, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

Al-Ashhab and al-Hasan read "bi-musmi'i man" with the genitive construction (idafa).

﴿You are only a warner.﴾ That is, your only duty is to convey and to warn. If the one being warned is among those whom God Most High wills to guide, he listens and is guided. And if he is among those whom He, glory be to Him, wills to go astray, and has sealed upon his heart, then you bear no responsibility for him.

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth.﴾ That is, as one who confirms the truth (muḥiqqīn), which is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) referring to the agent (fā'il), or as one who is confirmed in truth (muḥiqqan), which is a ḥāl referring to the object (maf'ūl), or as a sending accompanied by the truth, which is a ṣifah (qualifier) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be linked to His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿bearer of good tidings﴾. The complement of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and a warner﴾ is omitted, because the contrast indicates its counterpart: bearer of good tidings of the true promise, and warner of the true threat.

﴿And there was no nation﴾ That is, there is no large community of people of an age, and no nation of the nations that have passed through the past eras, ﴿but a warner had passed (khalā) among them﴾, that is, had gone by. This is either a prophet or a scholar who warns them. Mention of only the warner is sufficient, since it is known that warning is close to bearing good tidings, especially since they were mentioned together a little earlier, while warning is more fitting to the context. It was also said that the warner was singled out for mention because good tidings can only be known through hearing, so they are among the special characteristics of the prophets, peace be upon them. Thus the bearer of good tidings is a prophet or one who transmits from a prophet, unlike warning, which can be known through hearing and through reason. Therefore the warner is ascribed to every nation. There is a question about this.

Some people have taken as evidence this verse together with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies on its two wings, but that they are communities like you﴾ [al-An'am: 38], that among beasts and all other animals there are prophets or scholars who warn. The use of that as evidence is false, and its falsehood is so evident that it is hardly hidden from anyone, even from the beasts. We have not heard the claim that any single beast or the like is a prophet except from Shaykh Muhyi al-Din and those who followed him, may God sanctify his secret. I have seen in some books that saying so is disbelief, and we seek refuge in God Most High.
