﴿And there was no nation﴾ That is, there is no large community of people of an age, and no nation of the nations that have passed through the past eras, ﴿but a warner had passed (khalā) among them﴾, that is, had gone by. This is either a prophet or a scholar who warns them. Mention of only the warner is sufficient, since it is known that warning is close to bearing good tidings, especially since they were mentioned together a little earlier, while warning is more fitting to the context. It was also said that the warner was singled out for mention because good tidings can only be known through hearing, so they are among the special characteristics of the prophets, peace be upon them. Thus the bearer of good tidings is a prophet or one who transmits from a prophet, unlike warning, which can be known through hearing and through reason. Therefore the warner is ascribed to every nation. There is a question about this.

Some people have taken as evidence this verse together with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies on its two wings, but that they are communities like you﴾ [al-An'am: 38], that among beasts and all other animals there are prophets or scholars who warn. The use of that as evidence is false, and its falsehood is so evident that it is hardly hidden from anyone, even from the beasts. We have not heard the claim that any single beast or the like is a prophet except from Shaykh Muhyi al-Din and those who followed him, may God sanctify his secret. I have seen in some books that saying so is disbelief, and we seek refuge in God Most High.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 25:

﴿And if they deny you, then those before them also denied; their messengers came to them with clear proofs and with the Psalms and the Book giving light.﴾ [Lit. "those before them denied" — from the nations that were rebellious; so do not grieve over the denial of these people toward you.]

﴿جاءَتْهم رُسُلُهُمْ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as Abu al-Baqa' said, either without the particle qad or with it estimated, i.e., "those before them denied, while their messengers had come to them." ﴿بِالبَيِّناتِ﴾ means with the manifest miracles that indicate their truthfulness in what they claim. ﴿وبِالزُّبُرِ﴾ means like the scrolls of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). ﴿وبِالكِتابِ المُنِيرِ﴾ means like the Torah and the Gospel, on the intention of distribution (tafṣīl), meaning that some of them came with this and some came with that, not on the intention of combination (jam'), and that every messenger came with all that is mentioned, so that it would follow that every messenger had a book; and the number of messengers is far greater than the number of books, as is well known. The outcome of this is to prohibit the absence (khuluww, i.e., a messenger without a scripture). It is also permissible that by "the scrolls" and "the Book" is meant one thing, and the conjunction is for the difference of the two designations; but in this there is remoteness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 26:

﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved﴾. The apparent noun is placed in the position of their pronoun, to condemn them by what is in the relative clause (ṣilah) and to indicate the cause of the seizing. ﴿So how was My rejection﴾, i.e., My rejecting of them by punishment. In this there is additional emphasis and awe. The discussion of the like of this has already passed in (surah) Saba', so recall it.

And in the verse there is, regarding his consolation (ﷺ), what is in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 27:

﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ — water, etc. It is a resumptive statement (istinaf) directed at what comes to mind, to establish what His words indicated: ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, so how was My rejection?﴾ — of His great power, Mighty and Majestic is He. Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam, a title of the great jurist and exegete) said: it is to establish what preceded it concerning the differing of people, by showing that difference and variation is a constant matter across all created things, from plants, inanimate objects and animals.

Abu Hayyan said: it is an affirmation of His oneness through heavenly and earthly proofs, following the affirmation through the parables He struck, exalted is His majesty. This is as you see. The interrogative is for affirmation, and the seeing is of the heart (qalbiyyah), because the sending down of rain, although perceived by sight, is not so as to Allah's sending it down. The address is general, meaning: Do you not know that Allah, from the direction of height, sent down water ﴿and We brought forth thereby﴾, that is, by that water as a customary cause of bringing forth. It was also said: it means "We brought forth in its presence." The shift (iltifat) is to show full attention to the act, because of the wondrous craftsmanship in it, which indicates the perfection of power and wisdom.

﴿fruits of diverse colours﴾ — that is, their kinds, such as apples, pomegranates, grapes, figs and others that cannot be counted. This is like saying: so-and-so brought various kinds of stories, and he offered such-and-such a type of food. The variation within each kind is by the multiplicity of its varieties, as in apples, which have varieties differing in taste and appearance; the same applies to all other fruits, and there is hardly any kind of them without varieties that differ. It is also permissible that what is meant is the variation of each kind by the variation of its individual members.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah that he understood the colours (alwan) in their known meaning, and their variation as yellow, red, green and others. This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the most fitting to His words: ﴿And of the mountains are streaks, white and red﴾. It is either coordinated with what precedes it in meaning, or a circumstantial clause (hal); its being a resumptive statement, together with its connection to what precedes, is not evident. ﴿Judad﴾ is the plural of judda, with a damma, which is a streak (tariqah), from jaddahu when he cut it. Abu al-Fadl said: they are streaks whose colour differs from what is adjacent to them, and from this is the judda of the donkey, the line along the middle of its back that differs in colour from it. Ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about the judad, and he said: streaks, a white streak and a green streak. And he recited the poet's verse:

The beast has left upon their flanks streaks, as if they were roads that appeared upon the hills.

The phrase is on the assumption of an elided noun if the emphasis is not intended, since the mountains are not the streaks themselves; that is, possessing streaks.

Al-Zuhri read "jududun" with two dammas, plural of jadidah, like safinah and sufun, and it has the sense of jiddah. The author of al-Lawami said it is the plural of jadid, meaning new, clearly coloured traces. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the sense of "new" has no place in this verse. Perhaps whoever holds that mountains are continually newly coming into being and forming from waters that spring from the earth and harden little by little, then spring from a place near what has hardened so that it also hardens, and so on until a mountain results, does not object to reading the verse in this reading as mentioned.

The apparent meaning from the verses and reports is that Allah brought the mountains into being shortly after creating the earth, lest it sway with its inhabitants. The philosophers claim that they were mud in seas that receded and then hardened. The Imam (al-Razi) extended discussion on this in his book al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyyah and argued for it by the existence of marine things such as shells among their parts; but this, on close examination, is vain, and most of its proofs are mutilated. Whoever wishes to know what they said should return to their books. It is also related from him that he read "jadadun" with two fathas, but Abu Hatim did not permit this and said: this reading is not sound in meaning. Others declared it sound and said: al-jadad is the clear, evident road, but the singular was placed in the position of the plural, and therefore it is described with the plural. It was also said it is of the type of nutfah amshaj and thawb akhlaq, because the road comprises pieces.

It was objected that this is neither evident nor suitable for the plural of mountains. ﴿Differing in their colours﴾ — that is, their kinds, in intensity and weakness, because it is predicated by gradation (tashkik). So "mukhtalif" is an attribute of "bid" and "humr", and "alwanuha" is its agent, not its subject; "mukhtalif" is its predicate, since "mukhtalifatun" is then required. It is also permitted that it is an attribute of "judad", and "gharabib" is coordinated with "bid", so it is among the details of the streaks and the attributes subsisting in them; that is, and among the mountains are those possessing streaks, white and red, and gharabib. Al-gharbib is the one who has gone far in blackness and become extreme in it, and from it comes "al-ghurab" (the crow). Its use is frequent in their speech as a follower of "aswad" (black), either as its attribute or as a verbal emphasis, so they say: black, gharbib, as they say: white, yaqaq; yellow, faqi'; red, qani.

The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that "gharabib" here is an emphasis of an elided term, the original being "wa-sudun gharabib", i.e. intensely black. It was objected that this is valid only according to the view of one who permits the deletion of the emphasized term; among grammarians some prohibited this, and it is the choice of Ibn Malik, because emphasis requires care and reinforcement and the intent of lengthening, whereas deletion requires the opposite. Al-Saffar refuted this, as in the commentary on al-Tashil, because the deleted term, being indicated by a proof, is like the mentioned one, so it does not contradict its emphasis. In some commentaries on al-Mufassal it is stated that it is an attribute of that elided term, which was put in its place after its deletion.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿black﴾ is a substitute for it or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to it, and it explains the elided term. A parallel to this is the words of al-Nabighah:

And the one who protects the birds that the riders of Mecca wipe between al-Ghayl and al-Sanad.

In it there is explanation after ambiguity, and extra care in the description of blackness, since it is indicated by way of both implicature and explicit mention.

It is also permissible that the coordination is with "judad", in the sense: and of the mountains are those possessing streaks of differing colour, and of them are gharabib of uniform colour, as the contrast indicates; and the structure is brought out in the manner you have heard. And it seems that when he gave attention to the matter of blackness by conveying that it is at its utmost intensity, he did not mention after it the difference in intensity and weakness.

Al-Farra said: the speech is in inversion, that is, black gharabib. It was also said there is no emphasized term nor elided attribute, but rather "gharabib" is coordinated with "judad" or with "bid" from the outset, and "sud" is a substitute for it. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: this is good, and what makes it good is that gharbib was not required to be used as an emphasis. Among what came in the hadith is: Allah, exalted is He, dislikes the old man gharbib, who dyes with black; Ibn al-Athir interpreted it as the one who does not grey, that is, for his frivolity or for his lack of concern for the matter of his afterlife. What is in al-Bahr was related with the formula "it was said", and the verse of the poet:

The eye is aspiring, the hand is haughty, the leg is glistening, and the face is gharbib.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 28:

﴿And among men and beasts and cattle, their colours differ.﴾ That is: among them there are some whose colours differ, or some of them whose colours differ, according to what they said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among men are those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. The sentence is conjoined to the sentence before it, and its ruling is the ruling of that sentence.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that the presentation of the two sentences as nominal sentences, although they share with what precedes them, the verbal sentence, in citing its content for the diversity of people in inward states, is because the difference of mountains, men, beasts and cattle in the colours mentioned is a continuous matter, so it was expressed by what indicates continuity. As for the bringing forth of diverse fruits, since it is a matter that occurs anew, it was expressed by what indicates occurrence. Then, since there is in it a kind of obscurity, sight was attached to it by way of the interrogative of affirmation, which indicates urging toward it and encouraging it, unlike the states of mountains, men and others, for they are observed things that need no reflection; therefore they were stripped of attachment to sight. So reflect. End of quote.

What he mentioned about the matter of attaching sight is contrary to what is in al-Bahr, where he said: "This is an interrogative of affirmation, and it does not occur except regarding something extremely apparent. So reflect."

al-Zuhri read ﴿wa-l-dawabbu﴾ with the ba' lightened, exaggerating in fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), just as some of them made hamzah in ﴿wa-la l-daallin﴾ for the same reason.

[Page 191]

Ibn al-Sumayqa' read ﴿alwanuha﴾ (its colours). His words, ﴿kadhalika﴾ (likewise), are in the place of an accusative as an adjective of the verbal noun of ﴿mukhtalif﴾ (differing), which is emphasised, and the estimate is: "differs with a difference being as such", that is, like the difference of fruits and mountains. So it is part of the speech before it, and pausing upon it is good by the consensus of the people of recitation (ahl al-ada').

His words, glorified is He: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ complete His words: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18], by specifying who among men fears Him, exalted and majestic is He, after an allusion to explaining the nobility of fear and the baseness of its opposite, and a warning to those characterised by it, and a confirmation of His power, exalted and majestic is He, which calls for fear, as we say. Or after explaining the differing of classes of men and the diversity of their ranks: either in the abstract attributes, by way of likening (tamthil), or in the outward attributes, by way of explicit statement, giving each of the two its due fitting explanation. It was said that ﴿kadhalika﴾ is in the place of the nominative as the predicate of a deleted subject, that is, "the matter is thus", i.e., as it was explained and summarised. Then it was said: ﴿Only fears God﴾, etc., and it was taken in the manner of metonymy (kinayah), in the manner of the Arabs' saying "the Arabs do not break covenants", indicating that knowledge requires fear and is suitable to it. It is a transition to mentioning His friends, exalted is He, with the benefit that they are the ones among whom the warning was effective, and that you have, through them, sufficiency from these obstinate ones. The author of al-Kashf said: "The nominative is more apparent, so that it may be of the decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that ﴿kadhalika﴾ is connected to what follows it, coming out as a cause, that is: "Likewise, reflection and consideration upon God's creatures and the difference of their colours — the scholars fear God." Al-Samin refuted this, saying that innama does not govern what precedes it, and that pausing on ﴿kadhalika﴾ is agreed upon by the people of recitation. Al-Khafaji approved it and said: "By this the weakness of what was said becomes clear: that the meaning is 'the matter is thus', i.e., as it was explained and summarised, on the basis that it is a transition to mentioning the friends of God, exalted is He. But in this meaning there is no governing of what follows 'innama' over what precedes it, and the consensus of the people of recitation on pausing at ﴿kadhalika﴾, if granted, does not show by it the weakness of that." In some of the transmitted tafsirs from the early generation there is something that suggests the attachment of ﴿kadhalika﴾ to what follows it.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that he said regarding the verse: "Just as these cattle differ, people differ in the fear of God, exalted is He, likewise." This, in my view, is weak, and the more apparent is what the majority hold, and what was said is more subtle and refined.

By "the scholars" is meant those who know God, exalted and majestic is He, and what befits Him of His glorious attributes, His praiseworthy acts and all His beautiful affairs; not those who know grammar and morphology, for example. The basis of fear is that knowledge, not this mere acquaintance. So whoever knows Him, exalted is He, more, fears Him more.

al-Darimi transmitted from 'Ata' who said: Moses, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, which of Your servants is the most judicious?" He said: "The one who judges for people as he judges for himself." He said: "O Lord, which of Your servants is the richest?" He said: "The one most pleased with what I have apportioned to him." He said: "O Lord, which of Your servants fears most?" He said: "The one who knows Me best." And it is authentically related from him (ﷺ) that he said: "I am the one among you who fears God most, and the one who is most God-fearing toward Him."

Because it is the basis, fear was mentioned after what indicates the perfection of power. For this same reason Ibn 'Abbas explained, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir, the word ﴿the scholars﴾ in the verse as "those who know that God is powerful over everything." The placing of the object first is because the intent is to explain those who fear and to inform that they are specifically the scholars and no others. Had it been delayed, the intent would have been to explain the one feared and to inform that it is God and none other, as in His words: ﴿They fear no one except God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 39]. The context does not require this, but rather requires the first, so that it becomes an allusion (ta'rid) to the warners who persist in disbelief and obstinacy, and that they are ignorant of God and His attributes, and for that reason they do not fear God, exalted is He, nor fear His punishment.

Some have denied that ﴿innama﴾ here indicates exclusivity (hasr), and this is not correct. It is related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with them both, that they read: "Innama yakhsha Allaha" with ﴿Allah﴾ in the nominative and ﴿al-'ulama'a﴾ in the accusative. The author of al-Nashr criticised this reading. Abu Hayyan said:

[Page 192]

"Perhaps it is not sound from them both. We have seen books on the irregular readings (shadhdh), and they did not mention this reading; rather al-Zamakhshari mentioned it, and Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn 'Ali ibn Junadah mentioned it from Abu Haywah in his book al-Kamil." It was interpreted as: fear is a metaphor (majaz) for glorification, by the relation of necessary consequence, for the one glorified is awe-inspiring. It was said that fear occurs with the meaning of choice, as in the saying:

"I chose my paternal cousins, but I did not see their like..."

﴿Indeed God is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving﴾ is an explanation of why fear is obligatory, because might indicates perfection of power to take vengeance, and forgiveness and mercy are attributed only to one capable of punishment. It was said that ﴿Forgiving﴾ is mentioned by way of completion (takmil), like the example in the verse of al-Ghanawi mentioned just above.

According to some transmitted reports, the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, in whom fear was manifest, to the extent that he was known for it.

﴿Indeed those who recite the Book of God﴾: that is, they persist in reciting it until it became a mark of them and a title, as the form of the present tense indicates, and its occurrence as a relative clause, and the difference of the two verbs. By "the Book of God" is meant the Qur'an, for Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "This is the verse of the reciters."

'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi transmitted in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning Husayn ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib al-Qurashi. Then, the lesson is in the generality of the wording. Therefore al-Suddi said regarding the reciters: they are the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). 'Ata' said: they are the believers in general, and this is the more preponderant, and the Companions enter it primarily. It was said: the meaning of "recite the Book of God" is follow it, so they act according to what is in it, as if he took "yatlu" from "talahu" meaning "followed him", or he carried the familiar recitation to acting, since there is not much benefit in it without acting. It has been related: "How many a reciter of the Qur'an, while the Qur'an curses him!"

The statement of some of them suggests choosing the apparent meaning, where he said: when He mentioned fear, which is an act of the heart, He then mentioned after it the knowledge of the tongue, the limbs, and financial worship. It is permissible that by "the Book of God" is meant the genus of His books, exalted and majestic is He, which applies to the Torah, the Gospel and others, so that it would be praise of the believers among the nations after the narration of the state of the deniers by His words: ﴿And if they deny you﴾, etc. The present tense is for narrating a past state, and the purpose of praising them and explaining what they have is to urge this nation to follow them and to do as they did. The first meaning is more apt, as is not hidden, and the majority hold it.

﴿And they establish the prayer and spend of what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. That is, they spend while being secret and open, or in secrecy and openness. The intended meaning is that they spend in whatever manner occurs to them, without intending either of the two. It has also been said that secrecy applies to the recommended (*masnun*) spending and openness to the obligatory (*mafrud*) spending. That the spending is from what they were provided indicates that they did not waste and did not stretch their hands out fully. The context of praise also suggests that they sought out what is lawful and good. It has been said that *min* (from) is used for this reason. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school who held that God's justice requires certain consequences) restrict *rizq* (provision) to what is lawful, which is most fitting with the attribution of the verb to the pronoun of majesty. Whoever does not restrict it to the lawful says that it is for magnification and encouragement to spend.

﴿Yarjuna﴾ (they hope) for what they gave of acts of obedience, ﴿tijarah﴾ (a trade), that is, a transaction with God, Exalted, seeking the profit of reward. This is on the basis that *tijarah* (trade) is a metaphor for what has been mentioned, and the indicator (*qarinah*) is contextual, as some eminent scholars have said. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿lan tabur﴾ (it will never perish), that is, it will never become unsaleable (*taksud*). It has been said that it will never be destroyed by loss, as an attribute of *tijarah* and as *tarshih* (a supporting term that completes a metaphor). The clause ﴿yarjuna﴾ and what follows, according to al-Farra' and Abu al-Baqa', is the predicate of *inna*. In God's report about them with this, there is an indication that they are not certain that their trade will be lost, but rather they perform the acts of obedience they performed while their hearts are fearful that it will not be accepted from them. Some have made *tijarah* a metaphor for obtaining reward through obedience, with the matter of *tarshih* remaining as it is, and Abu al-Su'ud went to this view. Then he said: The report of their hope from the Most Generous of the generous is a definite promise that what they hope for will be attained.

Page 193

The apparent meaning of what has been narrated from Qatadah, in his interpreting *tijarah* as Paradise, is that it is a metaphor for profit. He interpreted ﴿lan tabur﴾ as "will never perish," and that is, as you see, not correct.

The Almighty's saying, ﴿That He may pay them their rewards﴾, is connected by some scholars to what is indicated by لَنْ تُعَلَّقَ (bi-ni'mati rabbika) in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You, by the grace of your Lord, are not a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2]. It is connected to what is indicated by (ma), not to the particle itself, since according to the well-known view a prepositional phrase is not attached to the particle. That is, the slump is negated from it, and it is circulated before God, that He may pay them the rewards of their deeds.

﴿And increase them of His bounty﴾ beyond that, from the treasuries of His mercy, what He wills. Abu Wa'il reported that His increasing them consists of granting them intercession for those they did good to. Al-Dahhak said it is by widening their hearts. In a hadith it is by multiplying their good deeds. It was also said it is by looking upon His Noble Face.

Apparently ﴿of His bounty﴾ refers to what is with Him, so it indicates that the paying of their rewards is like an obligation, because it is their recompense by His promise, glory be to Him. It is permissible that it refers to both, or that it is connected to an implied element indicated by what precedes it, namely what has been counted among their pleasing deeds, meaning: they did all that so that He would pay them their rewards, etc. It was also permitted that it be connected to what precedes it by the principle of tanazu' (the grammatical dispute over a shared element, i.e., two verbs competing for the same complement). Abu al-Baqa's treatment suggests a preference for connecting it to (yarjūna, "they hope"), and making the lam in it the lam of becoming (lam al-sayrura, indicating an outcome rather than a purpose). It is objected that there is no obstacle to taking it as the lam of cause (lam al-'illa), as is the common and widespread usage, and no apparent reason for departing from it.

al-Tibi justified this by saying that their aim in what they did was nothing but a commerce that does not slump, because the relative clause here is a cause and a declaration of the certainty of the report. When that led to God paying them their rewards, the lam was used. The reason some eminent scholars, such as al-Zamakhshari, did not take this view is that this lam is only found where the second element, which is what follows it, results from the first and is not intended, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is, according to most scholars, a justification of what precedes it, namely the full payment and the increase. That is, He is forgiving of the shortcomings of the obedient and appreciative of their acts of obedience, meaning He rewards them for these with the most complete reward. Thus He pays these people their rewards and increases them of His bounty. It is permitted that it be a predicate after a predicate, with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning "for them." It is also permitted that it be the predicate itself, with the returning pronoun implied. The clause ﴿they hope﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿spent﴾, based on the view that a restrictive qualifier following several items applies only to the last one, as is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. Or it may be because the hope for profitable commerce is more suitable to spending. Or it may be connected to an implied element, meaning: they did all of that while hoping.

al-Tibi preferred this, and on this view the clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah), so it is not objected that this creates a separation between the subject and its predicate by a foreign element. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿those who﴾, by way of tanazu'. The use of tanazu' with a circumstantial clause is not well known, but I see no harm in it. Some contemporary scholars preferred making the mentioned clause a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿spent﴾, because of its proximity and the strong fit between spending and hoping for a commerce that has circulation. It is not far-fetched that a parallel of it was omitted earlier, because it indicates it. Some also took ﴿that He may pay them﴾ as disputed between the three coordinated verbs, or took the clause as a circumstantial clause from an implied element, as you have just heard. Or ﴿and that He may pay them﴾ is connected to (yarjūna, "they hope"). The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is the predicate of the subject, and the connecting pronoun is omitted. In the clause ﴿they hope﴾ etc. there is the possibility of a parabolic metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), even if it is remote, and I have not seen anyone mention it, so reflect upon it.

﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ is the Qur'an. The particle *min* (مِن) here is for specification (*li-l-tabyin*), since the Qur'an is more specific in meaning than "that which We revealed," even though the two are identical in essence; or the phrase refers to the genus of the Book. The particle *min* may also be partitive (*li-l-tab'id*), since what is meant by "that which We revealed" is the Qur'an, which is part of the genus of the Book. It was said that it refers to the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh*), and then *min* is for origin (*li-l-ibtida'*).

﴿He is the Truth﴾. If the intended meaning is restriction (*qasr*), then it is restriction of the subject (*musnad ilayhi*) to the predicate (*musnad*), not the reverse, because the meaning would not be sound unless emphasis is intended. This was stated by al-Khafaji. The common and prevalent usage in such constructions is the restriction of the predicate to the subject. Here, if emphasis is not intended, it is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*) with respect to what the People of the Book fabricate and attribute to God Most High.
