﴿confirming what is before it﴾, i.e., the heavenly scriptures that preceded it. The word *musaddiqan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and its governing element is an implied one, understood from the meaning of the preceding clause; that is, "I establish it as confirming." It is an emphatic circumstantial clause (*hal mu'akkida*), because its being true necessitates its agreement with the divine books that preceded it in time, in beliefs and in the fundamentals of rulings. The *lam* is for reinforcement.

﴿Indeed, Allah is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾, encompassing the inner and outer aspects of their affairs. So if there were in your circumstances anything contradicting prophethood, such a true, miraculous revelation, which is a criterion (*'iyar*) over all the other books, would not have been revealed to you. The placing of *lakhabir* (All-Aware) first serves to alert that the essential matters are the spiritual ones. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this when he said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your deeds, but He looks at your hearts."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾, that is, the Qur'an, as the majority hold. The conjunction (ʿatf) is said to be upon "those We revealed" (alladhi awhayna), and it is said to be upon "We revealed" (awhayna), with the apparent noun standing in place of the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun. This latter view is preferred on the basis of proximity and the agreement of the two clauses. That is, "then We gave it" without toil or exertion in seeking it. ﴿Those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾. They are, as Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for Allah the Exalted chose them over all other nations, made them a middle nation so that they would be witnesses over mankind, and singled them out by affiliation to the most noble and excellent of His messengers, upon them be blessings and peace. The "then" (thumma) indicates a gradual sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), since the revelation of the Book to him (ﷺ) is more exalted than the inheritance mentioned, as though the latter were a consequence of it. Through it his prophethood was established, upon him be blessings and peace, which is the source of every good. It is not a temporal sequence (al-tarakhi al-zamani), because the time of its revelation to him, upon him be blessings and peace, is the time of its inheritance. His giving it to his community means specifying it for them and making it their Book, to which they return and by whose acting upon it they benefit. If by his causing them to inherit it is meant his conveying it from himself (ﷺ) and making them benefit from it, understanding what is in it directly, as the scholars do, or indirectly, as others after him, upon him be blessings and peace, then it is a temporal sequence. The expression of this in the past tense is due to its certainty.

It is also permitted that the meaning of "We caused the Book to be inherited" is "We decreed its inheritance and determined it," taking it as a metaphor through the use of the cause for the effect. In that case "then" indicates a gradation of rank, since otherwise the time of the decree precedes the time of the revelation. The reason for expressing it in the past tense on this view is clear.

In the commentary of al-Radi (Sharh al-Radi) it is stated that "thumma" may occur particularly in the conjunction of sentences to indicate that what follows is remote from what precedes and not fitting with it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him﴾ [Hud: 3, 90]. The distance between the repentance of servants, which is the servant's complete turning to Him, Exalted is He, and seeking forgiveness is a great gap. This meaning is a branch of temporal sequence, and its figurative use is as stated.

Ibn al-Shaykh (Ibn al-Shaykh al-Balqini?) made what is here like what is in this verse. He also permitted that "then We caused it to be inherited" etc. be connected to what preceded, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119] and ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. The meaning would be: "then We caused the Book to be inherited from the earlier nations, and gave it after them to those whom We chose from the Muhammadan community." The Book here is the Qur'an, as it has been said.

﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 196]. It has also been said that this need not be considered, and the meaning becomes: "then We delayed the Qur'an beyond the earlier nations and gave it to this community." The order of the discourse is that He, Exalted is He, first mentioned the sending of a messenger to every nation, and followed it with what indicates that those nations split into two factions: one faction denied the messengers and what was sent with them, and these are the ones referred to by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those before them denied, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and with the scriptures and the enlightening Book﴾ [Fatir: 25]. The other faction believed them, recited the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and acted in accordance with its requirements, and these are the ones referred to by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer﴾ etc. After He, Exalted is He, praised those who recite His books and act by His laws from among the deniers of the other nations, He came with what is specific to His messenger (ﷺ), namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that which We revealed to you of the Book﴾ etc., as a digression interposed. Then He informed, Exalted is He, of His causing this noble Book to be inherited by this community after the giving of the scriptures and the enlightening Book to those nations. On this view the meaning of "caused to inherit" is according to its apparent sense, and "then" indicates a sequence in the report or a sequence in rank, signifying the excellence of this Book over all other books and the excellence of this community over all other nations. On this view, the Book in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ is taken as a genus, and the verse is taken as praise of the nations that confirmed the prophets after recounting the state of those among them who denied. If this is objected to, it is in a good place.

It is also permitted that it be a conjunction upon ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾. If the inheritance of the Book preceded its recitation, then the meaning is according to its apparent sense, and "then" indicates a gradation in rank or a sequence in the report.

﴿And that which We revealed﴾ etc. is a parenthetical clause explaining the manner of the inheritance, for when it (the Qur'an) confirms them by agreeing with them in the creeds and fundamentals, it is as though it were they, and as though it had passed on to them from those who went before. This is as you see. It is also permitted, on this view and on the view before it, that the Book be taken as a genus, though it is clear that the intended meaning is the Qur'an.

It has been said that the intended meaning of "those chosen" is the scholars of the community, from among the Companions and those after them who follow their way, and their being caused to inherit the Qur'an means that He made them understand its meaning, become acquainted with its truths and subtleties, and become trustees of its secrets.

The Imamiyyah (Imami Shi'a) narrated from al-Sadiq and al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they said: "It is specifically for us, and it is us that is meant." They meant that the People of the House, or the Imams from among them, are the chosen ones who were caused to inherit the Book. Al-Tabarsi al-Imami chose this view and said in his tafsir (Majma' al-Bayan): "This is the closest of the opinions, for they are the most worthy of the description of being chosen and selected and of inheriting the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them."

It may perhaps be supported by his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Indeed I am leaving among you the two weighty things: the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and my family (ʿitrah). They will not part from one another until they come to me at the Basin (al-Hawd)."

But interpreting them as the scholars of the community is preferable to this specification, and the scholars of the People of the House enter it in the first place, for the Book was revealed in their house, and "they will not part until they come to the Basin on the Day of Reckoning." If the idafah (possessive construction) in ﴿Our servants﴾ is for honour, and "servants" is specific to the believers of this community, and "min" (from) is partitive, then interpreting "those chosen" as the scholars is almost required.

It is narrated from al-Jubba'i that they are the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah chose them and bestowed upon them His message and His books. On this view the definite article of "the Book" is generic, and the conjunction is upon His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that which We revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾, and "then" indicates a sequence in the report. He first informed of what our Prophet (ﷺ) was given, which includes information that he (ﷺ) was given the Book in the most perfect manner. Then He informed, Exalted is He, of the inheritance by his brother prophets, peace be upon them, and of their being given the books. One objection to this is that the giving of the books to the prophets, peace be upon them, is already known from His saying: ﴿Those before them denied, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and with the scriptures and the enlightening Book﴾ [Fatir: 25].

It is narrated from Abu Muslim that they are the chosen ones mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ [Al ʿImran: 33]. This is weaker than what came before. In any case, the relative pronoun is the first object of "caused to inherit," and "the Book" is its second object, placed first for its nobility, for attention to it, and to avoid ambiguity. "Min" is explanatory or partitive.

﴿Then among them is one who wrongs himself﴾. The "fa" (then) is for detail, not for causation, as has been said. The plural pronoun, as you heard earlier in explaining the relative pronoun, refers to the relative pronoun. The one who wrongs himself is one who fell short in acting upon the Book and was excessive against himself. This applies also to one who wrongs others, since by that he wrongs himself. The well-known opposite is the one who wrongs others, and the "lam" is for emphasis.

﴿And among them is one who is moderate﴾. He vacillates between acting upon it and opposing it, so he acts at times and opposes at other times. The original meaning of iqtisad (moderation) is being balanced in the matter.

﴿And among them is one who is foremost﴾, going forward toward the reward of Allah and His Garden, ﴿in good deeds﴾, that is, by means of good deeds, meaning righteous actions. It has been said: he is foremost over the one who wrongs himself and the moderate in ranks, by means of good deeds. It has also been said: he who attains excellence by means of them. ﴿By permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His facilitation and enabling, Exalted is He and Mighty and Majestic. In this is an indication of how difficult it is to attain this rank and how hard its acquisition is. It has been explained as the one whose obedience overcame his disobedience and whose action by the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, was abundant. What has been mentioned in explaining the three categories, which al-Hasan's words point to, is that he said: "The one who wrongs himself is the one whose good deeds are light; the moderate is the one whose good and bad are equal; and the foremost is the one whose good deeds outweigh."

Beyond this there are many opinions:

Mu'adh said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who died upon a major sin without repenting of it; the moderate is the one who died upon a minor sin and did not commit a major sin without repenting of it; the foremost is the one who died repentant of a major or minor sin, or who did not commit that at all.

It has been said: the one who wrongs himself is the disobedient and excessive sinner; the moderate is the one who avoids major sins; the foremost is the one who is godfearing absolutely.

It has been said: the first is the one who falls short in action; the second is the one who acts by the Book for the most part but is not free from mixing; the third are the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers.

It has been said: the first two are as mentioned, and the third is the one who constantly maintains the obligations of the Book in knowledge, action, and teaching.

It has been said: the first is one who accepted Islam after the conquest (of Mecca), the second is one who accepted it before that, and the third is one who accepted it before the Emigration.

It has been said: they are those who do not care from where they obtain (provision), whose sustenance is from what is lawful, and who are content from this world with mere sufficiency.

It has been said: whose concern is this world, whose concern is the hereafter, and whose concern is the Master (Allah).

It has been said: the seeker of salvation, the seeker of ranks, and the seeker of intimate converse.

It has been said: the one who abandons error, the one who abandons heedlessness, and the one who abandons attachment.

It has been said: he whose livelihood occupies him from his afterlife; he who is occupied with both; and he whose afterlife occupies him from his livelihood.

It has been said: he who performs the obligations out of fear of the Fire; he who performs them out of fear of it together with pleasure and seeking reward; and he who performs them only out of pleasure and seeking reward.

It has been said: the one who is heedless of the (prescribed) time and of congregation; the one who guards the time but not the congregation; and the one who guards both.

It has been said: he whose desire overcomes his intellect; he whose two are equal; and he whose intellect overcomes his desire.

It has been said: he who does not forbid wrong yet commits it; he who forbids wrong and commits it; and he who enjoins good and does it.

It has been said: the one of injustice, the one of justice, and the one of grace.

It has been said: the dweller of the desert, the dweller of the town, and the one who strives.

It has been said: he whose outward is better than his inward; he whose inward and outward are equal; and he whose inward is better than his outward.

It has been said: the reciter of the Qur'an who neither knows it nor acts by its requirement; the reciter who knows but does not act; and the reciter who knows and acts.

It has been said: the ignorant, the learner, and the scholar.

It has been said: he who opposes the commands and commits the prohibited; he who strives in performing the obligations though he is not granted success in that; and he who does not oppose the obligations of Allah, Exalted is He.

Some of the Imamiyyah narrated from Muyassar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "The one who wrongs himself among us is he who does not know the right of the Imam; the moderate is one who knows the right of the Imam; and the foremost is the Imam himself."

And from Ziyad ibn al-Mundhir, from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him: "The one who wrongs himself among us is he who did one righteous deed and another evil; the moderate is the devout and diligent worshipper; and the foremost in good deeds are ʿAli, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, and whoever of the family of Muhammad was killed as a martyr."

It has been said: they are the one who professes the oneness of Allah with his tongue while his limbs oppose it; the one who restrains his limbs by the obligations; and the one whom the realization of Divine Oneness makes forget everything other than that Oneness.

It has been said: he who enters Paradise through intercession; he who enters it through the grace of Allah, Exalted is He; and he who enters it without reckoning.

It has been said: he who is given his book from behind his back; he who is given his book in his left hand; and he who is given his book in his right hand.

It has been said: the unbeliever absolutely, the sinner, and the believing godfearing one.

In the same sense is what came in a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and ʿIkrimah: the one who wrongs himself are the companions of the left (al-mash'amah), the moderate are the companions of the right (al-maymanah), and the foremost in good deeds are the foremost, those brought near.

[Page 197]

It is apparent that these (scholars) and those who share their view take the pronoun in *minhum* ("from among them") to refer to *al-ʿibād* ("the servants"), not to the relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl*, "those whom We chose"). There is no doubt that among them are the disbelievers and others. The restriction of *al-ʿibād*, which is annexed to Allah, the Exalted, to the believers is not a consistent rule; it applies only when the annexation is intended to show honor (*al-tashrīf*). Holding that the pronoun refers to the relative pronoun, and committing to the view that the chosen status is according to natural disposition (*al-fiṭrah*), is a forced interpretation (*taʿassuf*), as is not hidden.

It has been said regarding the explanation of the three categories other than what has been mentioned. In *al-Taḥrīr* (Ibn ʿĀshūr's, or the work of Ibn al-Humām, as cited), he mentions forty-three opinions on this. Whoever surveys the exegeses will find them more numerous than that, but he will not find much real difference among most of them. What is supported by the majority of the narrations and reports is that the three categories are all among the people of Paradise. Therefore, one should not give heed to explaining *al-ẓālim* ("the one who wrongs himself") as a disbeliever, except by interpreting it as one who is ungrateful for blessings (*kāfir al-niʿmah*) and intending by it a disobedient person.

Imam Aḥmad, al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqī, and al-Tirmidhī (who graded it *ḥasan*) reported from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning this verse, ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾ up to ﴿with good deeds﴾: "These are all of one rank, and they are all in Paradise." The words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "and they are all, etc.," are an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf tafsīrī*).

Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh in *al-Baʿth* reported from Usāmah ibn Zayd that he said concerning the verse: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'All of them are from this Ummah, and all of them are in Paradise.'"

Ibn al-Najjār reported from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven."

Al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar to this.

Imam Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī reported from Abū al-Dardāʾ, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We have chosen from Our servants; so among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds by Allah's permission﴾. As for those who were foremost, they will enter Paradise without reckoning. As for those who were moderate, they will be reckoned with an easy reckoning. As for those who wronged themselves, they will be held back for a long time at the gathering place, and then they are those whom Allah will meet with His mercy. They are the ones who say, 'Praise be to Allah, who has removed grief from us; indeed our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative,'" etc.

Al-Bayhaqī said: When narrations are numerous for a hadith, it shows that the hadith has a basis. The reports on this subject are numerous, and what has been mentioned is sufficient.

The wrongdoer to himself (*al-ẓālim li-nafsihi*) is mentioned first because those who wrong themselves are numerous; the moderate is placed after him because the moderate are few compared to them; and the foremost is placed last because the foremost are fewer than the few. This is what al-Zamakhsharī said. Al-Ṭabarsī related that this order corresponds to the stations of people, for the states of the servants are three: disobedience, then repentance, then nearness (to Allah). When the servant disobeys, he is a wrongdoer; when he repents, he is moderate; and when his repentance is sound and his striving abundant, he is foremost. It has also been said: the wrongdoer is mentioned first so that he does not despair of Allah's mercy, and the foremost is mentioned last so that he is not deluded by his deed, so the placement of the moderate in the middle is determined. Quṭb al-Dīn said: The point in placing the wrongdoer first is that he is closest of the three to the beginning of the servant's state, before his being chosen by the inheritance of the Book. When the chosen status touches him, some servants are affected slightly, and they are the wrongdoers to themselves; some are affected moderately, and they are the moderate; and some are affected fully, and they are the foremost. Close to this is what has been said: the chosen status is graded (*mushakkak*), its levels vary, and its first level is what belongs to the believer who wrongs himself; above it is what belongs to the moderate; and above that is what belongs to the one foremost in good deeds. Thus the order comes like a progression through the levels. It has also been said: the foremost is placed last because of the multiplicity of what is connected to him; if he were placed first or in the middle, there would be a distance in general between the coordinated categories. And since moderation is like the relation between wrongdoing and foremost-ness, this requires placing the wrongdoer first and the moderate last, so that the moderate lies between the wrongdoer and the foremost in wording, just as he lies between them in meaning.

It may also be said: these three were ordered in this way to match their situation in mention relative to what they were promised of gardens in His saying, ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ up to the verse, their situation at the gathering when the promise is realized. The foremost, who enters the gardens first, is placed last so that his mention connects with the mention of the gardens promised, and the moderate is mentioned before him. The foremost is made a separator between him and the gardens, because he enters them only after him, so he separates him from them in entering. The wrongdoer to himself is mentioned before both because he enters them and connects with them only after both enter. Thus the delay of the foremost is, in meaning, a precedence, and the precedence of the wrongdoer is, in meaning, a delay. This may admit of other aspects that become clear upon reflection, so reflect.

Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, ʿUmar ibn Abī Shujāʿ, Yaʿqūb in one transmission, and al-Qazzāz from Abū ʿAmr read *sabbāq* ("very foremost") in the intensive form.

﴿That﴾, i.e., what has preceded of inheritance and choosing, ﴿is the great bounty﴾ from Allah, Mighty and Majestic; there is no role for acquisition (*al-kasb*) in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 33:

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿they will enter them﴾. This is supported by the reading of al-Jahdari and Harun, on the authority of 'Asim, "jannat" (جَنّاتِ) in the accusative, by way of ishtighal (the verb being implied, a construction in which a noun is governed by a verb suppressed in favour of a pronoun), meaning: they will enter gardens of perpetual residence, they will enter them. The possibility that it is in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "al-khayrat" (the good things) is remote, and in it there is the separation between the substitute and what it substitutes by an alien element, so it is not to be considered.

The plural pronoun (in "yadkhulunaha") refers either to "those whom We have chosen" (alladhina asfayna) or to the three categories. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That" is a reference to the foremost in good deeds (al-sabq bi'l-khayrat), and "gardens of perpetual residence" is a substitute for the grace (al-fadl), which is the foremost in good deeds. Since being foremost in good deeds is a cause for attaining reward, the reward itself was made to stand in place of the caused effect (al-musabbab) by treating the cause as its effect, and then it was substituted for it. The plural pronoun refers to the foremost (al-sabiq), because the intent is toward the category (jins), so the promise was particularized to the last category, out of deference to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (i'tizal). This applies, as you have heard, to the three categories. That is the more apparent in the sublime text, so that His statement afterwards, ﴿But those who disbelieved, for them is the fire of Hell﴾, corresponds to it, and so that it accords with the discourse of honour and distinction embedded in His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾. Otherwise, what honour is there in that mention after it has been necessary that most of those chosen are paired with the disbelievers? And so that the mention of the Forgiving (al-Ghafur) accords with the state of the wrongdoer (al-zalim), the moderate (al-muqtasid) and the thankful (al-shakur), and the state of the foremost (al-sabiq). Also, because of the strained nature of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) he mentioned and its distance from good taste. And how could it not be the more apparent, when the most excellent of the Messengers and the one to whom this manifest Book was revealed has explained it that way, as has passed just now? To this the great majority of his distinguished Companions and stars of guidance among mankind went, may Allah be pleased with them. Among them, in the sea (of knowledge), he counted 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda', Abu Sa'id and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi, in al-Ba'th, transmitted from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that he said, after reciting the verse: "I bear witness before Allah, exalted is He, that He will cause them all to enter Paradise." And more than one transmitted from Ka'b that he recited the verse up to ﴿fatigue﴾ and then said: "They have entered it, by the Lord of the Ka'ba." In another wording: "All of them are in Paradise. Do you not see that its aftermath is ﴿But those who disbelieved, for them is the fire of Hell﴾?" Yes, if by the wrongdoer to himself (al-zalim li-nafsihi) is meant the disbeliever, then it is impossible for the pronoun to return to what has been mentioned, and it is required that it return to the foremost and to the moderate, because what is intended by both is the category. But it is not fitting that this be intended after those reports.

Zarr ibn Hubaysh and al-Zuhri read "jannat 'adn" (جَنَّةُ عَدْنٍ) in the singular and nominative. Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" (يُدْخَلُونَها) in the passive voice, and it is also related from Ibn Kathir.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿they will be adorned therein﴾ (yuhallawna fiha) is a second predicate for "gardens", or a conditional (muqaddara) circumstantial clause (hal). It has been said that, because the occurrence is close after the entering, it is counted as concomitant. It is also read "yahlawna" (يَحْلَوْنَ) with an open ya' and a sukun on the ha', with the lam lightened, from "halat al-mar'a", so she is "haliya" when she wears jewellery, and it is said "jid halin" (a neck adorned) when it has jewellery upon it.

﴿of bracelets﴾ (min asawira): the plural of siwar, according to what is in al-Irshad. In al-Qamus: "al-siwar, like kitab and ghurab, is the bracelet, and its plural is asawir, and its plural is asawira, and sur, and su'ur." Using the term plural for the plural of a plural is common, so there is no contradiction. The siwar of a woman is arabicised, as al-Raghib said, and its origin is "dastwara". "Min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning they will be adorned with some bracelets, as if it were a part that has distinction and superiority over the rest of the parts. It is also permitted that it be explanatory (lil-bayan), since mention of adornment indicates an indefinite jewellery. It has been said that it is superfluous (za'ida), on the basis of what al-Akhfash holds, namely the permissibility of its being superfluous in an affirmative sentence. It has been said that it is a qualifier (na't) of an omitted object of "yuhallawna", and that the verb means "they will wear". "Min" in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿of gold﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyya). ﴿and pearls﴾ (lu'lu'an) is coordinated (ma'tuf) on the位置 (mahall) of "min asawira", meaning: and they will be adorned therein with pearls.

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited the verse and said: Indeed, upon them are crowns; indeed, the least of the pearls among them would illuminate what lies between the East and the West."

It has been said: it is coordinated on the omitted object, or it is accusative by a suppressed verb indicated by "yuhallawna", meaning: and they will be given pearls.

A group of the Seven readers read "lu'lu'in" (لُؤْلُؤٍ) in the genitive, coordinated on "dhahab" (gold), meaning: they will be adorned therein with some bracelets made of a combination of gold and pearls, by stringing grains of gold together with grains of pearls and making a bracelet from that, as is customary today in our lands; or by inlaying gold with pearls, as some stones are inlaid. It has been said: meaning, of gold in the purity of pearl. In this there is what there is of turbidity. Perhaps whoever says that there is no commonality between the gold and pearls of this world and the gold and pearls of the Hereafter except in name does not accept the arrangement (of stringing) or the inlaying, as is not hidden. "Lu'lu'an" is also read with the first hamza lightened.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾ (harir), meaning pure silk (ibrisim mahd), as in Majma' al-Bayan. Al-Raghib said: it is a thin garment. The change of style, in that He did not say "and they will wear therein silk" (harira), has been said to be to indicate that the existence of clothing for them is a certain matter, independent of explanation, since it is not possible for them to be without it; what needs explanation is what their clothing is. This is unlike the bracelets and pearls, which are not among the necessary essentials; for this reason, justice between wives is not required in them. Thus the explanation of their adornment was confined to its essence. Perhaps this is what prompted the placing of adornment before the description of the state of clothing. It has been said that this is to show that silk is their customary clothing, while preserving the form of the verse-endings (fawasil); but this is not the case.

﴿And they will say﴾, meaning "and they say", and the past form is used to indicate certainty. ﴿"Praise be to God, who has removed from us the grief"﴾: the grief of the turning of the heart and fear of the outcome, as related from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. Abu al-Darda' said: the grief of the terrors of the Resurrection and what befalls them there from wronging their own souls. Al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas: the grief of the Fire. al-Dahhak said: the grief of death, they say this when death is slaughtered. Muqatil said: the grief of relocation, they say this when they have settled in it. Qatada said: the grief that their deeds may not be accepted. al-Kalbi said: the fear of Satan. Samura ibn Jundab said: the grief of the livelihood of this world, bread and the like. From Ibn Abbas: the grief of calamities and ailments. It was also said: the grief of rent for the house. The more appropriate view is that what is meant is the category of grief in general, encompassing all the griefs of religion, this world and the Hereafter, and everything you have heard is by way of illustration.

It has already been mentioned in a hadith: "Those who wronged themselves are the ones who will say", that is, after God has received them with His mercy, ﴿"Praise be to God, who has removed from us the grief"﴾, etc., so do not overlook this.

It was also recited as "al-huzn" with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay', as mentioned by Jinah ibn Hubaysh.

﴿"Indeed our Lord is Forgiving"﴾ toward those who sin, ﴿"Appreciative"﴾ toward those who obey. Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding this: He forgave us our great sins and appreciated from us our small deeds. In the Kashshaf: The mention of "Appreciative" is an indication that these people have many good deeds, and it would have been fitting for him to say: the mention of "Forgiving" is an indication that they have many lapses, so that it would correspond to the distinction and the composition (nazm) would not be broken. But his school of thought prevented him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 35:

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence﴾, i.e., the abode of residence from which there is never any removal, and it is Paradise.

﴿By His bounty﴾, i.e., by His favour, His grace and His generosity, may He be glorified. For although works are a cause of entering Paradise in general, their causality is also by the bounty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since there is no inherent entitlement. Whoever knows that works are finite and transient, while the reward of Paradise is lasting and does not cease, will have no doubt that Allah, exalted is He, did not settle whoever settles in the abode of permanence except out of His pure bounty, may He be glorified.

Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., by His giving and His beneficence, from the expression "so-and-so has surplus (fudul) over his people and excellences (fawadil)." It is not from the bounty (fadl) which is condescension (tafaddul), because the reward is in the position of a wage that is owed, whereas condescension is like a voluntary gift, and in it there is of the Mu'tazili doctrine what there is.

﴿No fatigue (nasab) touches us therein﴾, i.e., toil, ﴿nor does weariness (lughub) touch us therein﴾, i.e., exhaustion and languor, and it is the result of toil. Its conjunction with it and the repetition of the negated verb is for emphasis in showing the negation of each of them; so said a group of the eminent scholars. Some of them said: nasab is bodily toil and lughub is mental toil. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah that he interpreted nasab as pain, and the statement is of the type of:

"You do not see the lizard (dabb) there hiding in its burrow."

The clause is a circumstantial (hal) phrase relating to one of the two objects of ahalla.

Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and al-Sulami read "lughūbun" with a fatha on the lam. Al-Farra' said: it is what one is fatigued by, like fatur and sahur (what is eaten at dawn and at breaking of the fast). It is also permissible for it to be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "no lughub of lughub touches us therein," like "the poetry of a poet," as if it described the lughub as having been exhausted, i.e., made weary and tired.

The author of al-Lawami said: it may be a verbal noun like qabul, and if you wish you may make it an adjective of a hidden subject, i.e., "a matter of lughub."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 36:

﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell; it will not be decreed for them,﴾ meaning: no judgment will be passed upon them of a second death, ﴿so that they die﴾ and thereby find rest from its punishment entirely. The reason al-Zamakhshari... [see below] — rather, the reason the verb is explained as "it will not be decreed" (lā yuqḍā) rather than "they will not die" (lā yamūtūna) is so that the statement does not become idle (yalghū), since if it were "they will not die, so that they die," the sense would be incoherent; and this interpretation requires a further explanation with "so that they find rest" (yastarīḥū).

The verb yamūtū is in the subjunctive as an answer to the negation, by the implicit particle an (anna is elided), and the intended meaning is the negation of the consequence due to the negation of the cause, i.e., there is no judgment of death, so how could there be death?

Ibn Mas'ud... [the text here reads: ʿĪsā and al-Ḥasan read "fa-yamūtūna" with the nūn, as a coordination (ʿaṭfan), as Abū ʿUthmān al-Māzinī said, upon "yuqḍā," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they are not given leave so that they may make excuses﴾, meaning: it will not be decreed for them, and they will not die.] ﴿And its punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, the punishment known to them; rather, whenever its flame subsides, its blaze is increased. The intended meaning is the perpetuity of the punishment, so this does not contradict their being punished with the zamharir (intense cold) or the like. The deputy subject of yukhaffafu is ﴿ʿanhum﴾ and ﴿min ʿadhābihā﴾ is in the place of the accusative, and the reverse is permissible. It was also permitted that min be superfluous (zāʾida), in which case the raising of its genitive object is required, as the deputy of the subject, according to what Abū al-Baqāʾ said. ʿAbd al-Wārith reported from Abū ʿAmr "wa-lā yukhaffaf" with the fāʾ vowelless, likening the separated to the joined, as in the poet's saying:

Today I drink without being culpable
﴿Thus﴾, meaning: like that dreadful recompense, ﴿We recompense every ungrateful one﴾, one who exaggerates in disbelief or ingratitude; there is no lighter or lesser recompense than it.

Abū ʿAmr and Abū Ḥātim, from Nāfiʿ, read "yujzā" with the yāʾ in the passive, and "kull" in the nominative as deputy of the subject. It was also read "nujāzī" with a nūn vowelled with ḍamma and an alif after the jīm.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 37:

﴿And they will cry out therein.﴾ It is an iftiʿal (reflexive verbal form) from al-ṣurākh (the outcry), which is the intensity of shouting. The original is yaṣtarikhūna, and the tāʾ was changed into ṭāʾ. It is used frequently for seeking help (istighatha), because one who seeks help generally shouts. Qatada interpreted it here in this sense, saying: "They will seek help therein." Their seeking help is directed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as indicated by what follows it. It has also been said that it is addressed to some of them because of their bewilderment, but this is not the case.

﴿"Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteous deeds, other than what we used to do."﴾ This is with an implied verb of saying, meaning "and they will say," either with conjunction or without it, the latter being an explanation of what precedes; or "saying," as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to their pronoun. Restricting the righteous deed by the mentioned description expresses regret over what they did of non-righteous deeds while acknowledging it, and indicates that their removal is for its correction; so the description is emphasizing. Also, because they used to think that they were doing good works, it is as if they said: "We will do a righteous deed other than what we used to think was righteous and then do it." Thus the description is restrictive.

Abu al-Baqa mentioned that ﴿righteous﴾ and ﴿other than what﴾ may both be two adjectives of an omitted infinitive (maṣdar) or an omitted object, and that ﴿righteous﴾ may be an adjective of an infinitive while ﴿other than what﴾ is the object of ﴿we will do﴾.

Whichever the case, the meaning is: bring us out of the Fire and return us to the world, and we will do righteous deeds. It seems they intended by righteous deeds: monotheism, obedience to the command of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and submission to him. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "﴿We will do righteous deeds﴾ means: we will say, 'There is no god but Allah.'"

﴿"Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would remember might remember therein?"﴾ This is a response from the side of Allah, exalted, and a rebuke to them in the Hereafter, when they say "Our Lord" etc. So it is by estimation: "Then We say to them" or "Then it is said to them: Did We not give you a life..." In some reports, they are answered with this after a period equal to the length of the world. The interrogative hamzah is for denial, and the waw is for conjunction upon an implied element required by the context. "Mā" is either a relative pronoun or a descriptive noun, meaning: Did We not grant you respite and give you a life, the life in which whoever wanted to remember might remember, i.e., the life in which whoever intended to remember could be enabled, and that intention of remembrance and reflection was realized in him.

Abu Hayyan said: "Mā" is a temporal verbal noun, i.e., "Did We not give you life in a period of remembrance?" This was criticized because the pronoun in ﴿therein﴾ rejects it, since it does not refer back to it except according to al-Akhfash's view that it is a noun, which is weak. Perhaps he makes the pronoun refer to the "life" understood from ﴿We give life﴾, but this is far-fetched.

Making "mā" a negation is not valid, as Ibn al-Hajib said, both verbally and semantically. This life, according to what is reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and related by a group and authenticated by al-Hakim from Ibn ʿAbbas, is sixty years. Al-Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and others related from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Allah, Exalted, has given an excuse to a man whose life He prolonged until he reached sixty years."

It has been said that it is fifty years. In one report from Ibn ʿAbbas, it is forty-six years. ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that it is forty years; in another report from him, it is the age of puberty. It has been said: seventeen years. From Qatada: eighteen years. From ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz: twenty years. From Mujahid: between twenty and sixty.

al-Aʿmash recited: "mā yadhdhakkaru fīhi," from iddhakkara with assimilation and with a hamzat al-wasl pronounced in continuous speech.

﴿"And there came to you the warner."﴾ It is conjoined to the meaning of the interrogative clause, as if it were said: "We gave you life and there came to you the warner." So it is not conjunction of a declarative upon an imperative, as in His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ and ﴿We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh: 1, 2]. It is also permitted that it is conjoined to ﴿We gave you life﴾, with the hamzah entering upon both, so do not be heedless.

By "the warner," according to what is reported from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It has been said: what came with him of the Qur'an. Abu Hayyan said: the intended meaning is the category of warner, and they are the prophets, peace be upon them; every prophet is the warner of his nation. This is supported by its being read as "al-nudhur" in the plural. From Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna, Waki', al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, al-Farra' and al-Tabari: it is white hair (grey hair). In a report: "No hair turns white except that it says to its sister: Prepare yourself, for death has drawn near." From here it was said:

I saw grey hair as one of the warnings of death to its owner, and that is enough of a warner for you.

And a speaker says to her: "Dye yourself, my beloved, and blacken the hair of your grey with perfume."
So I said to her: "Grey hair is the warner of my life, and I will not blacken the face of the warner."

It has been said: it is fever. It has been said: the death of relatives and kin. It has been said: the perfection of reason. The restriction to "the warner" is because it is what the context requires. The fa' in His saying, exalted: ﴿So taste﴾ is for ordering the command to taste upon what precedes it of the giving of life and the coming of the warner. And in His saying, glorified: ﴿So the wrongdoers have no helper﴾ it is for causation. By "wrongdoing" here is meant disbelief. It has been said the apparent wording would be "fa-mā lakum," but it turned to the explicit form for rebuke of them. The meaning is the continuing denial that they have any helper who would repel the punishment from them.

Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. That is, every unseen thing in them; nothing hidden in them is concealed from Him, glorified is He. Thus their circumstances, which wisdom required that they be treated in this manner and not be brought out of the Fire, are not hidden from Him, exalted is His station.

Jannah ibn Hubaysh read «عالِمٌ» with tanwin and «غَيْبَ» in the accusative, as the object (maf'ul bihi) of "ʿālimun."

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. It was said: this is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, because when He, exalted is He, knows the concealed things of the breasts, which are the most hidden of things, He, mighty and majestic, is more knowing of other than them. And in this there is a kind of concealment.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: the statement of the Exalted, "Indeed Allah..." etc., is a confirmation of their remaining in punishment, even though they disbelieved only for a number of counted days. It is as if a questioner asks about the reason for that, so it is said: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is not hidden from by the unseen of the heavens and the earth, so nothing in the breasts is hidden from Him. He, glorified is He, knows of the disbeliever that disbelief has taken firm root in his heart such that, if it lasted forever, he would never obey Allah, the Exalted, nor worship Him. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that the first clause is a reason for the second, the reverse of what was said. It is possible to say: the statement of the Exalted, ﴿So there is no helper for the wrongdoers﴾, includes the negation of their having a helper on a continuing basis, and it requires their abiding in punishment. So it could invite the question: how is that negated on a continuing basis, when custom among the witnessed affairs dictates that there is a helper for one whose days of punishment are prolonged? It is answered: Indeed Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, in the sense that He, exalted is He, encompasses things in knowledge; so if they had a helper at any time whatsoever, He would know it, and would not have negated it on a continuing basis. Likewise, it could invite the question: how are they made to abide in punishment when they wronged only for counted days? It is answered: Indeed He is Knowing of what is within the breasts, in the sense that He, exalted is He, knows what their hearts conceal, so He knows that they have resolved upon the misguidance and disbelief they are in forever. Thus each of the two clauses is a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani). So reflect.

﴿He it is who has made you successors upon the earth﴾. The meaning is: the keys of disposal and benefit from what is in it have been handed over to you. Or: He has made you successors of those nations who came before you, and has made you inheritors of the worldly goods that are in your hands, so that you would give thanks to Him by affirming His oneness and by obedience. Or: He has made you a replacement for those nations before you who denied the messengers and were destroyed, so that you would take heed from their condition and from the destruction that befell them.

The address is said to be general, and al-Bahr (*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit* by Abu Hayyan) favours this view. It is also said to be addressed to the people of Makkah. *Khala'if* is the plural of *khalifa*, and the plural pattern *fa'a'il* is regularly used for the form *fa'ila* (a pattern of plurals). As for *al-Khulafa'*, it is the plural of *khalif*, like *karim* and *kurama'*. Al-Wahidi permitted that it is also the plural of *khalifa*, though this is contrary to what is well known.

﴿So whoever disbelieves﴾ among you, having ignored this noble blessing, or whoever persists in disbelief and abandons faith after He has shown kindness to him and provided him with what alerts him to what follows from that. ﴿Upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning the burden of his disbelief and its recompense, not upon anyone else.

﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them, in the sight of their Lord, except in hatred﴾, meaning the utmost contempt, detestation and wrath.

﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss﴾ in the Hereafter. The clause ﴿does not increase﴾ and what follows is an explanation and elaboration of His statement ﴿upon him is his disbelief﴾. For the sake of further detailing it, it has been placed in the position of something distinct from it; were it not for this, it would have been joined to it. The repetition serves to add emphasis and to draw attention to the point that disbelief, by itself, requires each of the two matters, namely hatred and loss, independently to require its ugliness and the obligation to avoid it. The meaning is that if disbelief entailed nothing other than the hatred of God, Exalted is He, that would suffice to establish its ugliness; and likewise, if it entailed nothing other than loss, that would suffice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 40:

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them: ﴿Tell me about your associates whom you call upon besides Allah﴾, meaning your gods. The attribution to them is due to the slightest connection, since they are the ones who made them partners of Allah, the Exalted, and believed them to be so without any basis whatsoever.

It has also been said: the attribution is genuine, in that they made them partners for themselves in what they possess, or Allah, the Exalted, made them partners for them in the Fire, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. The qualifier in both cases is restrictive, not emphatic. The context and the preceding and following passages of the noble verse clearly point to what came before.

﴿Show me﴾ what ﴿they have created from the earth﴾. This is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution by inclusion) from ﴿Tell me﴾, because it has the sense of "inform me," as if it were said: "Inform me about your partners, show me what part of the earth they created, so that they deserve divinity and partnership." It was also permitted that it be a badal kull (substitution of the whole). Abu Hayyan said: the substitution is not permitted, because if something that the interrogative particle has entered upon is substituted, the particle must enter upon the substitute as well. Also, substituting a clause for a clause is not attested in their speech. Furthermore, the substitute operates on the basis of repeating the governing word, and this cannot apply here because there is no governing word for ﴿Tell me﴾. He then said: "What I hold is that ﴿Tell me﴾ means 'inform me,' and it requires two objects, one of which is in the accusative and the other of which contains the interrogative, like the Arabs' saying: 'Tell me about Zayd, what he did.' So the first here is ﴿your partners﴾ and the second is ﴿what they created﴾. ﴿Show me﴾ is a parenthetical clause containing emphasis and reinforcement of the speech. It is possible that this is also a case of i'mal (government of the second of two verbs), since ﴿what they created﴾ is governed by both ﴿Tell me﴾ and ﴿Show me﴾, for ﴿Show me﴾ has been linked from its second object, just as ra'a (to see), which was not preceded by the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza), is linked from its object in their saying: 'Do you not see what lightning is here?' The second verb is then governed according to the preferred view of the Basran grammarians." Yet what he mentioned is only one possibility in the noble verse, just as what was mentioned first is also a possibility. His rebuttal is worthless. As for the first point, the necessity of the particle entering upon the substitute applies when the interrogative retains its meaning; when it is neutralised from it, as here, that is not necessary. As for the second, the grammarians and the scholars of semantics have explicitly stated otherwise, and it does occur in the speech of the Arabs, as in his saying:

I say to him: "Depart, do not stay with us, otherwise be a Muslim in secret and in public."

As for the third point, the basis of the substitute operating through repetition of the governing word is, as al-Khafaji reported from them, specific to substitution of single words. You cannot say that the governing word here exists, namely ﴿Say﴾, because what matters is the thing said, and there is no governing word for it, as is clear.

It was also permitted that ﴿Tell me﴾ does not mean "inform me," but rather that the intended meaning is the genuine interrogative about seeing, and ﴿Show me﴾ is an imperative of challenge for clarification, meaning: "Do you know what this thing you call upon is, and in what state of impotence it is? Or do you imagine that it has power? If you know it to be powerless, how can you worship it? Or if you imagine it has power, then show me its effect." What preceded is more apparent.

﴿Or do they have a share in the heavens?﴾ That is: rather, do they have a partnership with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the creation of the heavens, such that they deserve what you claim about them? Some of them said: it is better not to supply an omitted noun (muda'f), so that the meaning is: "Or do they have a partnership with Him, glorified is He, in the heavens, in creating, sustaining and disposing?" because what is intended is the negation of the signs of divinity from the partners, and these signs are not restricted to creation. The supplied reading is more consistent with what precedes it. The discourse is said to proceed by gradation from independent ownership to partnership, and then from partnership to a clear proof written by way of partnership. As if it were said: "Inform me about those you call upon besides Allah: did they independently create any part of the earth such that they deserve to be worshipped like Allah, the Exalted? Rather, do they have a partnership with Him, glorified is He, in the creation of the heavens?"

﴿Or have We given them a Book?﴾ That is: rather, have We given them a Book that declares that We have taken them as partners, ﴿so they are upon a clear proof from it﴾, meaning a manifest argument from that Book that they have a partnership with Us.

Al-Kashshaf said: the apparent point is that the discourse is built on ascending gradation in establishing partnership, because independent creation of a part of the earth is a kind of partnership with Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and partnership with Him, glorified is He, in the creation of the heavens is more indicative of it, and then the giving of a Book from Him, the Exalted, that they are His partners is more indicative still and even more so. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿We have given them﴾ refers to the polytheists, and so does the one in ﴿so they are﴾, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ [al-Rum: 35], etc. So there is an iltifat (shift) in the speech from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence, turning away from the polytheists and treating them as absent.

The meaning is that the worship of these people is either based on reason, but no reason judges the worship of one who creates no part of the earth as valid, as a sign of partnership in the heavens; or based on transmission, but We have not given the polytheists a Book containing a command to worship these. In this there is a dislocation of the pronouns (tafkik al-damair).

Some said: the pronoun in ﴿We have given them﴾ refers to the partners, like the preceding pronouns, while the pronoun in ﴿so they are upon a clear proof﴾ refers to the polytheists. ﴿Or﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), marking a turn away from the preceding speech. He claimed that in that case there is neither iltifat nor tafkik. So reflect.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read ﴿clear proofs﴾ in the plural. This indicates that shirk is grave, and that it requires the reinforcement of many proofs. It is a form of mockery (tahakkum).

﴿Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion.﴾ When He, glorified is He, negated the arguments He negated in this matter, He turned away from it, the Mighty and Majestic, by mentioning what drove them to shirk, namely the ancestors' endorsement to the descendants and the misleading of the leaders of the followers by claiming that they are intercessors with Allah, the Exalted, who will intercede for them through their drawing near to Him. According to most, the verse concerns worshippers of idols, though its ruling is general. It was also said: it concerns those who worship other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whether an idol, a king, or other than these two.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, Allah holds fast the heavens and the earth lest they cease [to exist]﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) establishing the extreme ugliness of shirk, and it is [a clause] of its own. That is, Allah, exalted is He, preserves the heavens and the earth, [out of] aversion to their cessation, or lest they cease and vanish. For just as the contingent (mumkin) needs the Necessary Being, glorified is He, at the moment of its bringing into existence, so it needs Him at the moment of its continuance.

Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿yumsik﴾ means yamna' (prevents), and ﴿an tazulа﴾ is its object by elision and conveyance, because it is transitive with min, i.e., He prevents them from ﴿ceasing﴾." In al-Bahr, it is permissible that ﴿an tazula﴾ be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the heavens and the earth," meaning: He, glorified is He, prevents the cessation of the heavens and the earth.

Some have interpreted zawal as moving away from a place: that is, Allah, exalted is He, prevents the heavens from moving from their place so that they rise or sink, and He likewise prevents the earth from moving in that manner. There is a report narrated by 'Abd ibn Humayd and a group [of scholars] from Ibn 'Abbas that supports this.

It has also been said: their zawal is their rotation, so they are [themselves] stationary, and the revolving bodies with the stars are their orbits (aflak), which are other than the heavens. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Shaqiq, who said: It was said to Ibn Mas'ud that Ka'b said: "The sky revolves on a pivot like the pivot of a millstone on the shoulder of a king," and he said: "Ka'b lied. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds fast the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾, and it is enough of cessation that it should revolve."

The preferred view among the early scholars (al-salaf) is that the heavens do not revolve and that they are other than the orbits. Many of the later Muslim thinkers (al-Islamiyyin) held that they do revolve and that they are not other than the orbits. As for the earth, there is no disagreement among Muslims regarding its stillness, while the philosophers differ, and most of them hold it to be still; some of them held that it is in motion and that rising and setting are by its movement, but this has been refuted in its proper place. The better interpretation of the verse is what you have heard first, and likewise its being placed in the context we mentioned. It has also been said that when He, exalted is He, explained the corruption of the matter of the associates and established the proof of their invalidity, He followed that with His greatness, mighty and majestic is He, and His power, glorified is He, so that the thing becomes clear by its opposite, and the insignificance of the idols is confirmed by mention of the greatness of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And if they were to cease﴾: that is, if they were to approach ceasing, by way of supposition and assumption. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla, "and if they were to cease" (wa-law zalata). It has also been said that this points to what will happen on the Day of Resurrection of the folding up of the heavens and the crumbling of the mountains.

﴿No one can hold them after Him﴾: that is, no one holds them (ma amsakahuma) from anyone after Him, meaning after His holding them, or after the cessation. The clause is the answer to the implied oath preceding the lam of preparation (lam al-tawti'a) in "la'in" (wa-la'in), and the answer to the conditional is omitted, the answer to the oath indicating it. Amsaka here means yumsik, as in His saying, ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145]. The first min (in "min ahad") is extra, for emphasizing generality, and the second min is for the beginning (of the limit).

﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving﴾: therefore He forbears toward the polytheists and forgives those among them who repent, despite the greatness of their crime, which would require hastening the punishment and the failure to hold the heavens and the earth and the ruin of the world in which they are. So it should not be imagined that the context requires mention of power rather than forbearance and forgiveness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 42:**

﴿وأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ﴾ That is, they swore and exerted themselves in swearing, to bring it about with the utmost of their ability.

﴿لَئِنْ جاءَهم نَذِيرٌ لَيَكُونُنَّ أهْدى مِن إحْدى الأُمَمِ﴾ The pronouns refer to Quraysh. This is because they had learned, before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ), that a group of the People of the Book had denied their messengers. They said: "May God the Exalted curse the Jews and the Christians! Messengers came to them and they denied them. By God, if a messenger comes to us, we shall surely be better guided than any one of the nations." Then some of them did what they did, and God the Exalted revealed this verse. ﴿لَئِنْ جاءَهُمْ﴾ (*in ja'ahum*, "if he comes to them") is in the third person according to the sense, since they had said "*ja'anā*" (if he comes to us). Likewise "*layakūnunna*" (they will surely be). *Iḥdā* (one of) has the meaning of *wāḥidah* (one). The apparent sense is that it is general, even though it is indefinite in the affirmative, because the context requires generality. The definiteness of ﴿الأُمَمِ﴾ (the nations) is for a known reference, and the intended meaning is the nations that denied their messengers. That is: if a warner comes to us, we shall surely be better guided than each one of the nations, the Jews, the Christians and others, so that we all believe and none of us denies. Or the meaning is: we shall surely be better guided than a nation that is described as "one of the nations," as a way of preferring it over the other nations. This is like saying "he is the one of his people" or "the one of his age," and like their saying "he is the one of the two ones" and "she is the one of the ones," meaning preference in supplication and intellect. The poet said:

*Until they consulted me, the one of the ones,*
*A lion, fierce, bearing weapons, aggressive.*

Ibn Malik stated in *al-Tashil* that it may be said of something that is magnified and has no equal that it is "the one of the ones." However, al-Damamini said in his commentary: the use of *iḥdā* and similar words is established only when it is added to a plural taken from its own root, as in "*iḥdā l-iḥad*" (the one of the ones) and "*aḥad al-aḥadayn*" (the one of the two ones), or when it is added to an attribute, as in "*aḥad al-ʿulamāʾ*" (one of the scholars) and "*iḥdā l-kibar*" (one of the greatest). As for its addition to nouns of kind, such as "*al-umam*" (the nations), it requires transmission (from the Arabs). It was objected that the use of *iḥdā* for magnification without any addition at all is established, for they say of a great calamity: "*hiya iḥdā min sabʿ*" (it is one of seven), that is, one of the nights, meaning it has become severe and spread. They also say "*wāḥid qawmihi*" (the one of his people) and "*awḥaduhum*" (the most unique of them) and "*awḥadu ummihi*" (the most unique of his mother's children). No distinction has appeared between what is added to a plural taken from the word, what is added to an attribute, and what is added to nouns of kind. I do not think such a case requires transmission, so let it be considered.

The author of *al-Kashf* said: the indication of ﴿إحْدى الأُمَمِ﴾ (one of the nations) for preference is not clear, unlike "*wāḥid al-qawm*" (the one of the people) and the like. Then he explained it as following the style of:

*Or the death of some souls is bound [to them].*

He means that the indeterminate part may be intended for magnification, as with indefiniteness, so *iḥdā* is like it. In this it should be noted that once its use for magnification is established, its indication of preference becomes most clear.

﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهم نَذِيرٌ﴾ And what a warner! He is the most noble of the messengers, Muhammad (ﷺ), as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah, and this is the apparent meaning. From Muqatil it is reported that it is the splitting of the moon, but that is less evident than the Pleiades, and the context rejects it. ﴿ما زادَهُمْ﴾ (it did not increase them), that is, the warner or his coming, ﴿إلا نُفُورًا﴾ (except aversion), distancing from the truth and fleeing from it. Attributing the increase to that is metaphorical, since it is the cause of it. The clause is the answer to it (the *lammā*).

The verse has been cited as evidence that *in* (the negative particle) is a particle (*ḥarfiyyah*, that is, a non-verbal particle), because of the negation it contains, which prevents what follows it from operating on it. There is discussion on this point.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 43:**

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿in arrogance on the earth﴾, are a substitute (badal) for ﴿aversion﴾. Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent reading is that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), meaning that it is the reason for the aversion." The first view (that it is a substitute) is reported from al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "being arrogant."

﴿The evil plotting﴾ is the deception they intended against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the scheming against him. Qatadah said that it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was also reported from Ibn Jurayh. It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿arrogance﴾. The original construction is "and if they plot an evil plot," with ﴿evil﴾ being an adjective of an implied noun, meaning "a harmful plot." Then the verbal noun (masdar) was put in place of "an" with the verb, and it was made an annexed construction (idafah) to what had been the adjective. It is also permitted that it be coordinated with ﴿aversion﴾.

Al-A'mash and Hamzah read "al-sayyi'" with the hamzah silenced in connected speech, treating it as if it were in pause (waqf), or to avoid a sequence of vowels (tawali al-harakat), and treating the separated word as if it were joined to what follows. Al-Zajjaj claimed that this reading is a grammatical error (lahn), because it omits the case ending (i'rab), as Abu Ja'far also said. Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) claimed that omitting the case ending is not permitted in prose or poetry, because the case vowels were introduced to distinguish meanings. Some grammarians considered it too grave that al-A'mash should have read this way and said: "He only paused on this word, and the one who transmitted from him made a mistake. The proof of this is that it is a complete utterance, and for this reason he did not read the similar form in this way, even though the vowel there is heavier, since it is a damma between two kasras." But the truth is that it is not an error. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) gave many examples and arguments in al-Hujjah in support of the silent reading, for the sake of avoiding a sequence of vowels and connecting words with the intention of pausing.

Ibn al-Qushayri said: "Whatever is established by widespread transmission (istifadah) or by mass transmission (tawatur) as having been recited in this way must be permitted, and it cannot be called an error. By my life, the silent reading here is better than the silent reading in ﴿your Creator﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], as in the reading of Abu 'Amr."

It is reported from Ibn Kathir: "wa-makra al-sa'y" (with a silent hamzah after the sin and a kasra-vowelled ya after it), which is a metathesis (maqlub) of the lightened form of "al-say'" from ﴿al-sayyi'﴾, as the poet said:

*They do not repay good with evil, nor do they repay harshness with gentleness.*

Ibn Mas'ud read "makran sayyi'an" (a plot, an evil one), coordinating an indefinite noun with an indefinite noun.

﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass﴾, that is, it does not surround ﴿anyone except its own people﴾. Al-Raghib said: that is, it does not strike or descend. In any case, it is only used for what is disliked. Some claimed that the original form of ḥāqa was ḥaqqa, and one of the two identical letters was replaced by an alif, as in dhamma and dhāma, and zalla and zāla. This is an instance of an unrestricted proverb (irsal al-mathal). Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it headfirst." It is reported from Ka'b that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "I read in the Torah: 'Whoever digs a pit falls into it.'" He said: "I found that in the Book of Allah the Exalted." Then he recited the verse. And in a report: "Do not plot, and do not help a plotter, for Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾. Do not transgress, and do not help a transgressor, for Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Your transgression is only against yourselves﴾." The plotting of these people has indeed encompassed them on the Day of Badr.

The verse is general according to the sound view, and matters are judged by their outcomes. Allah the Exalted gives respite but does not neglect. Behind this world is the Hereafter, and ﴿those who have wronged will know what a return they will be returned to﴾. In sum, whoever is plotted against by another, and the plot takes effect against him quickly in appearance, is in reality the one who succeeds, while the plotter is the one who perishes. I ask Allah the Exalted, by the sanctity of His beloved, the Greatest (ﷺ), to repel and lift from us the plotting of the plotters, and to deal with them in both abodes with His justice. He, glory be to Him, is the Strong, the Firm.

It is also read "wa-la yuḥīq" (with a damma on the ya) and "al-makra al-sayyi'a" (in the accusative), on the basis that it is from aḥāqa, which is transitive, and its subject is a pronoun referring back to Allah the Exalted, while "al-makr" is its object.

﴿So do they await﴾, that is, do they wait for, and this is a metaphor by treating what is to come as what is awaited and expected, ﴿except the way of the former peoples﴾, that is, except the sunnah (way) of Allah the Exalted regarding them, by punishing those who denied them.

﴿So you will not find any alteration in the way of Allah﴾, by which He, glory be to Him, would put punishment in place of its proper place, ﴿and you will not find any transference in the way of Allah﴾, by which He would transfer His punishment from the deniers to others. The fa' (so) indicates the cause of what the ruling implies, namely their waiting for the punishment to come. The negation of finding alteration and transference is an expression for negating their existence by way of demonstrative proof (burhani). Singling out each of them with a separate negation is for emphasizing their non-existence. The address is general, or specific to him, upon whom be blessings and peace.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 35, verse 44:

﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ This is an proof for what precedes it, namely the continuation of God the Exalted's custom (sunnah) of punishing the deniers, by means of what they witness in their journeys and trade-travels in their caravans to al-Sham, Yemen and Iraq, of the traces of the past nations and the signs of their destruction. The hamzah is for rebuke (inkar), and the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element that suits the context, according to one opinion; that is, "Have they sat idle and not traveled?"

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were greater than them in strength﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with qad implied or without it.

﴿And God is not such as to be frustrated by anything﴾, meaning it is not within the nature of His exalted majesty that anything should outpace Him or escape Him, ﴿anything﴾, i.e., any thing, and "min" is for the comprehensiveness of things (istighraq al-ashya'), ﴿in the heavens or on earth﴾. This is parallel to ﴿Neither leaves behind a small one nor a great one﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. The waw is either circumstantial (hal) or conjunctive (ʿatf). In al-Irshad, the sentence is an interjected clause (i'tiraDh) confirming what is understood from what precedes it regarding the annihilation of the earlier nations, and its apparent sense is that the waw is interjectional (i'tiraDiyyah).

﴿Indeed, He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾, intensive in knowledge and power, and the clause is a justification (ta'lil) for the negation of frustration.

﴿Were Allah to take mankind﴾ all of them ﴿to task for what they have earned﴾, that is, for the evil deeds they committed, ﴿He would not leave upon its back﴾, that is, upon the back of the earth, ﴿any creature.﴾ The earth was already mentioned in His words, ﴿in the heavens or on the earth﴾. So the pronoun here is not a pronoun referring to something after its mention, as al-Radi (Radi al-Din al-Astarabadi) claimed. "The back of the earth" is a metaphor for its surface, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) and others said. It has also been said that the expression contains an implicit (makniyya) metaphor of imagination (takhyiliyya), and that what is meant is that He would leave on it ﴿any creature﴾, that is, any living being that crawls upon the earth, because of the ill omen of sins. He, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. This is also what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. It has also been said that by "creature" (dabba) is meant only humankind. This is supported by His words, ﴿but He defers them until a specified term﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun then refers to mankind, since it is the pronoun for rational beings, and the Day of Resurrection is the term set for the continuance of their species. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to all that has been mentioned, by way of precedence (taghlib), and the Day of Resurrection is the term set for the continuance of the kind of created beings.

﴿So when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾, so He will then recompense the accountable among them for their deeds: if it is evil, then evil, and if it is good, then good. The clause ﴿indeed Allah﴾ and what follows is placed in the position of the apodosis (jaza'), while the apodosis in reality is what is recompensed, as we have indicated. This is it, and Allah, Exalted is He, is the Granter of success for good, and there is no reliance except upon Him.
